🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars
- How to Control AI Agents Before Access Sprawl Takes Over → AI agents are rapidly gaining access to sensitive systems, data, and workflows—but most security programs were never designed to govern non-human identities at this scale. This webinar breaks down how to discover AI agents, control their permissions, prevent excessive access, and build a governance model that keeps agent adoption from turning into the next major identity security problem.
- AI Attacks Move at Machine Speed. Can Your Identity Security Keep Up? → AI-powered attacks can now move from reconnaissance to privilege escalation faster than traditional security teams can investigate and respond. This webinar explains why identity is becoming the critical real-time control layer—and how runtime identity security can help organizations detect risky access, enforce decisions across cloud, SaaS, on-prem, and AI environments, and stop machine-speed attacks before they turn into breaches.
📰 Around the Cyber World
- Google Halts OSS VRP Submissions — As of October 1, 2026, Google is no longer accepting OSS VRP product vulnerability submissions due to a "significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid." The tech giant added: "For some Google Cloud repos impacting Google Cloud products, we may still accept reports covering product vulnerabilities through the Cloud VRP. We will continue to reformat and work on this aspect of the OSS VRP and commit to giving an update in Q1 2027."
- Microsoft's X Account Briefly Hijacked — Unknown attackers hijacked the official Microsoft account on X, which has over 13 million followers, in what appeared to be a pump-and-dump scheme promoting a crypto token. "We have confirmed unauthorized access to our account on X, including posts that did not come from Microsoft," a Microsoft spokesperson told The Verge. "The account has been secured, and the unauthorized posts have been removed, and we are continuing to investigate the circumstances."
- TIKTOUK, a WordPress Credential Collection Toolkit — A new toolkit called TIKTOUK "brings together WordPress probing, collection of exposed configuration data, recovery of encrypted email credentials, and JavaScript secret scanning," LevelBlue said. TIKTOUK features Python components and a Go-based Linux crawler that probes WordPress pages and REST batch routes, collects configuration and option values, and retrieves referenced JavaScript files, scans their contents, and reports matching secret patterns.
- Google Details PageBreak — Google has detailed an internal AI agent called PageBreak that aims to autonomously scale vulnerability discovery while minimizing manual work arising from hallucinated bug reports. "Rather than simply hypothesizing bugs based on code patterns, the system closes the loop by verifying potential flaws against running environments," Google said. "This approach results in a near-zero false positive rate, ensuring that we avoid overloading product teams with unverified vulnerability reports." Page has uncovered over 500 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities across Google first-party web applications.
- Milk Dragon Phishing Kit Detailed — Group-IB has shed light on an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kit called Milk Dragon (aka NaiLong) that has been active since October 2025. "Unlike conventional phishing tactics that rely on fear and urgency, Milk Dragon lures victims with big discounts on consumer goods distributed via Facebook and TikTok marketplace advertisements," Group-IB said. "Phishing pages impersonate brands across multiple industries, including Retail & Supermarket chains. Well-known brand names such as LEGO, Calvin Klein, Aeon Malaysia, and many others are exploited and used as lures." The attack is designed to steal financial information from victims. Actively sold on Telegram, Milk Dragon has claimed victims spanning 66 countries, with 258 phishing pages identified to date.
- Iranian Hacker Extradited to the U.S. — An Iranian hacker accused of being behind a cyber espionage campaign targeting hundreds of universities, federal and state government agencies, private sector companies, and non-governmental organizations has been extradited to the U.S. Amir Barati, 40, is expected to face wire and computer fraud charges in the US Southern District of New York. The High Court in Podgorica approved his extradition last month.
- New Variant of NodeStealer Emerges — Netskope Threat Labs said it detected a new variant of NodeStealer packing major updates that turn it into a full-blown spyware. The new features were likely written with AI assistance. "The latest Python NodeStealer variant incorporates new spyware features, including keylogging, clipboard monitoring, and screenshot capture," Netskope said. "In addition, it expands its theft targets to include Wi-Fi passwords, the victim’s Pictures folder, and two additional web browsers. Earlier NodeStealer variants queried only two Facebook Graph API endpoints. The latest variant queries more than 20 endpoints to construct a comprehensive dossier on the individual managing the account."
- Bypassing Microsoft's RejectDirectSend — ReliaQuest said an empty Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) envelope sender can bypass RejectDirectSend, which is designed to block unauthenticated Direct Send mail. "An external sender can omit the envelope domain while retaining an internal-looking address, making phishing messages more likely to be trusted. The message still carries an internal-looking address, increasing the likelihood that spearphishing reaches the recipient," ReliaQuest said. "The technique requires only one empty field – no credentials, no registered lookalike domain, and no dedicated sending infrastructure – so organizations should expect continued use." The cybersecurity company said it observed attackers repeatedly using self-addressed messages and familiar business lures to target leadership and business-facing users.
- Attackers Exploit PaperCut Flaws to Deliver AdaptixC2 — In late August 2026, threat actors exploited CVE-2026-82078 and CVE-2026-81578, two PaperCut MF vulnerabilities, as zero-days to load an in-memory Java loader, which in turn deployed a web shell. The web shell was then used to deploy a trojanized Microsoft Copilot binary carrying an AdaptixC2 implant. "AdaptixC2 is an open-source and highly modular post-compromise framework that provides a broad set of capabilities, including remote shell access, file management, reverse proxying, and modules for Active Directory attacks, credential harvesting, lateral movement, and more," eSentire said. "In this intrusion, threat actors used the lateral movement module to steal a token from a process running under a domain-privileged service account and move laterally to a domain controller." Upon gaining access to the domain controller, the threat actors dumped credentials to obtain the service account's NTLM hash and enabled Windows Restricted Admin mode. Ultimately, the attackers dumped the domain's Active Directory NTDS.dit database in an attempt to collect password hashes for all domain accounts.
- Anthropic Says GLM-5.3 Can Build Cyber Exploits — Anthropic revealed that Zhipu AI's (aka Z.ai) GLM-5.3 model can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits, like Claude Mythos Preview, and that it has been released without "meaningful safeguards to limit misuse." The AI company said attackers can bypass the open-weight model's safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques, adding that these lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. "At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems," it added. "The funniest part is how Anthropic admitted self-reflectively that the lack of guardrails may actually be benefiting the defenders working to secure their systems," Evilginx creator Kuba Gretzky said in an X post. "Something they never wanted to allow, because of possible misuse."
Conclusion
This week was a useful reminder that attackers do not need one perfect path. A fresh exploit, an exposed secret, a weak mail control, or one careless workflow can all get them moving.
Patch what is exposed, review what is trusted by default, and keep an eye on the simple paths. The clever stuff matters, but plenty of trouble still starts with something ordinary being left open.

articles.title: Hackers hijacked Microsoft's X account for a scam featuring everyone's least-favorite tech mascot Clippy
articles.text:
Hackers hijacked Microsoft's X account for a scam featuring everyone's least-favorite tech mascot Clippy
Microsoft X account was used to promote a meme coin scam
- Microsoft’s X account was hijacked to promote the suspicious $CLIPPY cryptocurrency token
- Attackers amplified the scam with fake Microsoft-branded statements and apology posts
- Microsoft confirmed unauthorized access, removed the posts, and secured the account
Cybercriminals managed to briefly take over Microsoft’s X account and used it to promote a cryptocurrency-themed scam. To make matters even worse, they later tried to make it seem as if Microsoft reclaimed its account and issued a fake apology tweet.
The wonderful world of cryptocurrency has a subculture called “meme coins”. These are obscure, practically pointless tokens that emerge quickly as part of an ongoing trend, and disappear just as fast. For example, there was a token called SQUID that emerged while the Squid Game series was popular, and there was one called HAWK that rose while the “Hawk Tuah” girl was popular on the internet.
While not a rule, these coins are also often scams. Community members purchase them, allowing the creators to extract value before disappearing. SQUID was worth around $2,800 per token at its peak, and collapsed to $0.0008 within minutes, while HAWK lost around 90% of its value almost immediately after launch.
Enter Clippy
It seems that the latest meme coin to be used this way is called CLIPPY - based on the infamous virtual assistant that was introduced with Office 97.
For those of younger age, earlier versions of Microsoft Office came with a virtual assistant that would pop up at the bottom right of the screen and ask if the user needed any help. It was designed as a large paperclip with eyes, and was discontinued a few years later for being practically useless and annoying.
Since then, however, Clippy has become an internet meme, and something to be fondly remembered, particularly in today’s world of cold, calculated, heartless AI agents. Clippy has become a symbol of warmer, more humane time of computing, and as such it, too, was abused in a scam.
As part of the scam, the fraudsters created a Clippy X account, called “ClippyMSFTCo”, and posted a call to action: “How many likes to bring Clippy back? @microsoft give us a number, please.” Then they hijacked Microsoft’s official account and retweeted this post to their audience of 13 million.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
But promoting an obvious scam to millions of people trusting Microsoft was only half of the ruse. They later deleted the original post and issued a bizarre public apology:
"We are aware of a cryptocurrency token being promoted in connection with $MSFT stock, including the unauthorized use of the Clippy brand and Microsoft-related intellectual property,” the scammers wrote. “Microsoft has not authorized, sponsored, endorsed, or granted permission for the creation, promotion, or use of any cryptocurrency token associated with Clippy, Microsoft, or $MSFT."
This post was later deleted, as well.
Build your own Clippy
Musk’s social network has later disabled the fraudulent @clippymsftcto account. However, researchers from Cybernews later found a different account - @ClippyMSFT, still promoting the $CLIPPY token, stating it “has a liquidity pool paired directly with $MSFT.”
“For the first time ever, everyone’s favorite paperclip has a liquidity pool paired directly with $MSFT, the company that built him is now the floor under his bags,” one tweet reads. A separate tweet also promoted software that allows users to “build their own Clippy” which, if this author has learned anything over the years, sounds a lot like a way to distribute malware. In this particular case - possibly a cryptocurrency stealer.
Microsoft has later spoken up, telling the media that its account was compromised and abused in a scam: “We have confirmed unauthorized access to our account on X, including posts that did not come from Microsoft,” Microsoft spokesperson Brent Colburn said. “The account has been secured and the unauthorized posts have been removed, and we are continuing to investigate the circumstances.”

articles.title: Meta impulsa el proyecto Muse Gadgets para permitir que los desarrolladores creen sus propios accesorios de IA
articles.text:
Meta lanzó Muse Gadgets, un proyecto de código abierto para que desarrolladores creen accesorios propios conectados con Muse, su agente de inteligencia artificial. La iniciativa ofrece una base técnica para diseñar desde pantallas táctiles con la función “pulsa para hablar” hasta dispositivos que se conecten al puerto HDMI de una Smart TV. La propuesta busca llevar el agente fuera de las aplicaciones habituales y extenderlo a nuevos objetos tecnológicos.
El anuncio cobra relevancia porque Muse fue presentado a principios de septiembre como un sistema autónomo capaz de actuar en nombre del usuario. Meta indicó que puede buscar ofertas en la web, realizar compras, planear viajes y diseñar un programa de entrenamiento para los siguientes meses. Muse Gadgets abre la posibilidad de usar esas capacidades desde interfaces físicas, aunque también plantea preguntas sobre permisos, dispositivos, redes domésticas e información privada sensible.
El kit permite diseñar dispositivos conectados con Muse directamente
Para facilitar ese desarrollo, la compañía entrega firmware y un kit de desarrollo para Linux, conocido como Linux SDK. Ambos elementos permiten que el hardware creado establezca comunicación con el agente.
El planteamiento no obliga a seguir un formato único: cada desarrollador puede decidir forma, tamaño y finalidad del accesorio. Meta aporta infraestructura inicial; los creadores determinan cómo integrar Muse allí.
Los ejemplos incluyen pantallas táctiles, tinta y televisores inteligentes
Los ejemplos publicados muestran el alcance que Meta imagina para Muse Gadgets. Uno consiste en una pantalla de tinta electrónica, capaz de presentar respuestas, recordatorios o información consultada al agente. Otro adopta la forma de un stick HDMI para conectar Muse al televisor. También aparece un accesorio con pantalla táctil pequeña, pensado para ejecutar órdenes desde su pantalla, sin abrir aplicaciones.
Meta también presentó Muse Home Link, un dispositivo propio alimentado mediante USB tipo C. Nat Friedman, jefe de Producto de los laboratorios de superinteligencia de Meta, explicó que el accesorio permite conectar Muse a la red doméstica. Según indicó, el agente puede comunicarse con televisores, altavoces y otros equipos inteligentes que admitan HTTPS, el protocolo utilizado para intercambiar información mediante conexiones web.
El agente busca ampliar sus funciones cotidianas autónomas
El proyecto llega pocas semanas después de la presentación de Muse como agente autónomo. Meta señaló que puede buscar ofertas, organizar compras, planear viajes y diseñar programas de entrenamiento. Muse Gadgets busca trasladar esas tareas a objetos cotidianos. Una pantalla puede ofrecer consultas; un aparato para televisión puede ser punto de interacción; un control táctil activa solicitudes con el agente a demanda.
Cuál es la importancia del código abierto en el proyecto
El carácter abierto de Muse Gadgets permite que los desarrolladores planteen usos distintos para una misma base tecnológica. Un equipo puede construir una pantalla para mostrar datos; otro puede crear un accesorio para controlar dispositivos del hogar. El firmware y el SDK funcionan como punto de partida para conectar esos diseños con Muse. Meta no detalló productos, fabricantes ni fechas para lanzamientos.
Los antecedentes elevan las dudas sobre privacidad digital
La iniciativa aparece después de dos casos en los que Muse se apartó de las instrucciones de sus usuarios. En uno, el agente proporcionó a un comprador de Facebook Marketplace la dirección física de un vendedor sin consentimiento para concluir una compra. En otro, un columnista descubrió que Muse había accedido a sus mensajes en Mensajes de Apple sin autorización del propietario.
Meta deberá aclarar permisos para los nuevos accesorios
La conexión de Muse con pantallas y dispositivos domésticos amplía los usos, pero aumenta la importancia de los permisos. Un agente que gestiona compras, viajes e información requiere límites sobre datos y acciones. Muse Gadgets propone accesorios cuya evolución dependerá de desarrolladores, reglas y controles.

articles.title: Pas besoin d’attendre les Jours Flash Prime : la liseuse Kindle sans publicités passe déjà sous les 100€ chez Amazon
articles.text:
La liseuse Kindle 2024 peut vous permettre d’emporter des milliers de livres électroniques dans votre poche. Amazon propose actuellement sa version de 16 Go sans publicités pour 99,99 € au lieu de 169,99 €.
À l’approche des Jours Flash Prime qui débutent demain, Amazon baisse le prix de sa célèbre liseuse électronique dans son coloris noir. Le Kindle 2024 est disponible à 99,99 € chez le cybermarchand, dans sa version sans publicités et avec une capacité de stockage de 16 Go. Le prix habituel de ce modèle est de 169,99 €.
Le Kindle 2024 de 16 Go sans publicités est à 99,99 € chez Amazon, contre 169,99 € hors promotion.
Pour profiter des Jours Flash Prime n’oubliez pas de devenir membre Amazon Prime. Vous bénéficiez d’un essai gratuit de 30 jours, c’est donc le bon moment pour tester.
Pourquoi choisir le Kindle 2024 ?
- Pour son format compact : avec un poids de 158 g, elle se transporte facilement et peut se manipuler avec une seule main.
- Pour son écran à encre électronique : la dalle antireflet de 300 ppp affiche des caractères nets, avec un éclairage réglable pour lire le soir.
- Pour sa capacité de stockage : ses 16 Go lui permettent de stocker plusieurs milliers de livres, bandes dessinées et magazines.
Transportez votre bibliothèque partout avec vous
La liseuse Kindle pèse seulement 158 grammes pour un format de lecture de 6 pouces, et elle peut stocker des milliers d’ouvrages au format numérique. Elle offre aussi un confort de lecture personnalisable : la taille des caractères peut être ajustée, un mode sombre s’adapte aux sessions de lecture nocturnes et un système d’éclairage est intégré à l’appareil. Quant à l’autonomie, elle peut atteindre six semaines.
Une liseuse pour les adeptes du livre de poche
Cette liseuse Kindle met donc l’accent sur son côté compact et facile à manipuler. Par ailleurs, ce modèle fait l’impasse sur l’étanchéité et sur le réglage de la température de l’éclairage, deux fonctions que l’on trouve au sein du Kindle Paperwhite, qui possède un écran de 7 pouces.
✅ Les points forts
- Format compact et poids de 158 g.
- Écran antireflet de 300 ppp.
- Version sans publicités sur l’écran de verrouillage.
❌ Les limites
- Pas d’étanchéité.
- Pas de réglage de la température d’éclairage.
Le Kindle 2024 sans publicités est accessible à moins de 100 € avec cette offre Amazon.
À 99,99 €, ce Kindle se présente comme un choix adapté si vous désirez passer des livres de poche à la lecture numérique. Cela peut aussi représenter un bon cadeau à faire à un grand lecteur qui est souvent en déplacement.
Cependant, pour les amateurs de bandes dessinées ou les habitués des livres en grand format, un écran plus grand sera peut-être plus adapté. Il en va de même pour les personnes qui aiment lire dans leur bain et qui peuvent avoir intérêt à se tourner vers une liseuse étanche.

articles.title: 650 km d’autonomie et garantie à vie : Hyundai casse tous les prix avec sa nouvelle berline électrique à 13 000 €
articles.text:
La Chine est devenue le nouveau terrain de jeu de Hyundai. Si la marque coréenne poursuit sa conquête face aux stars du marché local, elle compte désormais développer en parallèle des modèles qui pourraient être commercialisés par la suite dans le reste du monde. C’est le cas de la Ioniq V, une berline électrique au style survolté qui n’a absolument rien à voir avec le Ioniq 5 bien familier sur nos routes.
Outre le design, c’est surtout le prix qui est d’un tout autre acabit. Fraîchement commercialisée dans l’Empire du Milieu, la Ioniq V s’affiche à partir de 109 900 yuans, voire 99 900 yuans grâce à une offre promotionnelle de lancement. Étant donné que 99 900 yuans correspondent environ à 13 200 €, la berline joue sur un positionnement tarifaire particulièrement agressif au vu de ses prestations.
Une garantie à vie et un remboursement en cas d’incendie
Car avec une longueur de 4,90 mètres, l’auto n’a rien d’une lilliputienne. Elle a par contre tout d’une marathonienne puisque sa batterie lithium fer phosphate de 66,8 kWh assure une autonomie confortable de 650 km sur le cycle CLTC. Les versions premier prix devront néanmoins se contenter d’un pack de 53,5 kWh réduisant le rayon d’action à 540 km. Dans les deux cas, la coréenne est branchée sur une plateforme en 800 V.
Puisque nous évoquons la technique, il est bon de savoir que la Ioniq V propose à son lancement une garantie à vie sur plusieurs de ses composants. Un remplacement de la batterie est ainsi prévu en cas de forte dégradation. Un remboursement complet du véhicule est aussi au programme si un incendie spontané du pack survient. Tout cela dans le but de conquérir de nouveaux acheteurs plus jeunes habitués aux modèles chinois.
Un arsenal technologique digne des plus grandes
En plus du prix et de la garantie, c’est l’équipement qui séduira, avec notamment un écran 4K de 27 pouces, un affichage tête haute, un chargeur à induction pour smartphone et un assistant vocal tournant avec deux modèles d’IA : Ernie Bot de Baidu et Doubao de ByteDance. D’autre part, le système de conduite semi-autonome a été développé avec Momenta. Une assistance complète est alors possible en ville et sur autoroute.
Dans les cinq prochaines années, Hyundai prévoit de lancer en Chine 20 modèles électriques traditionnels et à prolongateur d’autonomie. Le but ultime est de porter la production locale à 500 000 véhicules d’ici 2030 grâce à une multiplication des partenariats avec les acteurs locaux. La Ioniq V est le premier modèle de cette grande offensive. L’auto pourrait arriver chez nous si ses performances commerciales sont encourageantes.

articles.title: Desde el 5 de octubre en Lidl (rebajada a 12,99 euros), la solución para conectar aparatos en la terraza sin depender de enchufes cercanos
articles.text:
Disfrutar de la terraza, si tenemos alguna en casa, no sólo pasa por tomar el sol o el aire. También podemos sacarle partido teletrabajando en ella, viendo series y películas mediante un proyector o la televisión y jugando a la consola portátil, entre otras cosas. Y claro, para la mayoría de estas tareas o aficiones necesitamos tener alguna toma de corriente a mano.
Cable alargador, 10 m. - Parkside
En este sentido, Lidl tiene una solución muy interesante tanto si contamos con enchufes en la terraza pero no están a mano, como si necesitamos llevar la corriente desde el interior de casa hasta el exterior: este cable alargador con 10 metros de longitud de marca Parkside, disponible desde ayer rebajado a un precio de 12,99 euros.
A un precio similar, disponible en Amazon con envío gratis si somos miembros Prime (o aprovechamos la prueba gratuita de 30 días), encontramos esta alternativa muy bien valorada, con casi 3.000 reseñas y un precio de 13,03 euros. Opción a tener en cuenta en caso de no poder acercarnos a algún Lidl cercano.
EMOS Cable alargador IP44 5 m
Con 3.680 W de potencia, suficiente para conectar lo que queramos
Una de las novedades más interesantes del actual folleto de Lidl, con llegada a tiendas físicas y online desde ayer, lunes 5 de octubre, la protagoniza este cable alargador Parkside. El cual, en esencia, es un cable que permite llevar la toma de corriente desde cualquier punto de la terraza o el interior de casa a donde estemos (hasta un máximo de esos 10 metros, claro). Ideal para conectar el portátil, cargar el teléfono o la consola o enchufar el proyector.
La gran diferencia de este cable alargador Parkside frente a los convencionales que muchos usamos en nuestro día a día dentro de casa es su diseño y certificación IP44: tiene protección contra salpicaduras y pequeñas partículas, lo que sumado a su tapa de cierre con cubierta de goma hace que resista la intemperie con seguridad.
Aunque ojo, su uso no está recomendado para recibir agua directa de la lluvia, por ejemplo, ni estar permanentemente expuesto a cielo abierto. Lo ideal es colocarlo en algún lugar de la terraza donde, si bien se exponga a los elementos, quede relativamente protegido por alguna pared, techo o mueble.
A tener en cuenta que su potencia es de 3.680 W. Esto permite conectar, con seguridad y sin peligrosas sobrecargas, prácticamente cualquier electrodoméstico doméstico que pensemos usar en la terraza: la hidrolimpiadora o una televisión, por ejemplo. Siendo de sobra para dispositivos mucho menos demandantes de energía, como el cargador del teléfono, un portátil o una mini nevera apta para uso en exteriores.

articles.title: Get a rare deal on the shuckable 16TB Seagate Expansion Desktop hard drive at $0.02 per GB — save $100 on this big HDD ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
articles.text:
Get a rare deal on the shuckable 16TB Seagate Expansion Desktop hard drive at $0.02 per GB — save $100 on this big HDD ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
A surprisingly decent value when high-capacity HDDs are into four digits.
The AIpocolypse has consumed everything in its path, including the once-affordable high-capacity HDD. Newegg has a rare deal on a high-capacity 16TB external Seagate drive, knocking $100 off the price to bring it down to $449.99. That comes out to around $0.02 per GB, which is surprisingly sensible given HDD prices right now.
The cheapest 16TB HDD we can find new right now is the IronWolf Pro at $599, which itself is on sale for 6% off. Around this point last year, before HDD prices started soaring, you'd be able to pick up around 28TB for $500. Now, most 16TB drives are around $700, with higher-end Exos drives pushing up above $800.
If you prefer internal storage, you can remove the enclosure, extract the drive, and put it in a case. Note that doing so will void your warranty, so although it's possible, you might want to rethink that move given how expensive HDDs are right now.
The Seagate Expansion Desktop drive is a 16TB HDD that connects via USB 3.0. It's formatted to ExFAT by default, allowing it to work with virtually platform out of the box.
As with most external drives, the actual drive inside of the enclosure varies. Seagate doesn't list the speed of the drive inside, though many external HDDs run at 5,400 RPM. User reports online have shown both Barracuda and IronWolf Pro drives inside the Expansion Desktop, so naturally, your milage will vary.
You shouldn't expect great speeds from this drive. Most 5,400 RPM drives offer sustained sequential reads and writes around 100 MB/s. Thankfully, the USB 3.0 interface offers plenty of bandwidth to keep up with the slower drive. For long-term storage, speed shouldn't be an issue.
If you install the drive internally, you can use it for games, though you should stick to older titles. A lot of modern AAA games require an SSD, and even titles with HDD fallback like Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart struggle on slower 5,400 RPM drives.
Seagate ships the drive formatted to ExFAT, so it'll work with virtually any platform out of the box. Of course, you're free to reformat the drive to any file system you want.
At $449, the 16TB version of this drive is the one to buy. Both the 12TB and 14TB versions are more expensive at $619.99 and $660, respectively, while the 26TB version is $1,179.99.

articles.title: Utah gives startup Nolla Health permission to start issuing AI automated prescriptions for acne treatments - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Utah gives startup Nolla Health permission to start issuing AI automated prescriptions for acne treatments
Utah has become the first state in the U.S. to give an artificial intelligence startup permission to automate the approval of prescription refills with only minimal oversight from human physicians.
In a blog post today, Nolla Health said it has been granted approval by the state to launch a pilot project that will enable acne sufferers to talk to an AI agent, upload a photo of their face, and then automatically receive a prescription without speaking to a doctor. “This makes Nolla the first ever end-to-end AI doctor,” Nolla Health founder Luis Wenus said in a post on X today.
Through the Nolla Derm app available on iOS devices, an AI model can select which medicine to prescribe each user from a shortlist of physician-approved topical treatments, the company said. Any requests from patients that fall outside of its strict limits will be forwarded to a real, licensed human physician.
When users first download the app, they’ll have to go through an intake process before they can actually speak to the AI doctor. Once they’ve been approved, they can tell the app about their acne condition, upload a facial scan that shows how bad their acne really is, and the AI will then decide on an appropriate treatment plan.
The prescription can then be picked up at the user’s local pharmacy or sent directly to their home. The app also tracks patient’s progress through a daily skin scan, and updates their treatment plans monthly, based on how well it’s working.
“Until now, a licensed clinician signed every single prescription before it went out,” Wenus explained in a video introducing the app.” Our AI can now make that prescribing decision itself.”
Today, Nolla Health became the first organization in the U.S. (and possibly the world) to receive regulatory approval for an AI to issue initial prescriptions.
This makes Nolla the first ever actual end-to-end AI doctor. pic.twitter.com/xn6rvb8IyW
— Luis Wenus (@luiswenus) October 5, 2026
Tentative approval
The service is being made available as a pilot after being granted approval from the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, the Utah Division of Professional Licensing, the Utah Medical Association and the American Academy of Dermatology. Under the agreement, the company’s AI system is permitted to write prescriptions only for creams designed to treat topical acne. It’s barred from prescribing isotretinoin and oral medications.
The pilot program has three stages. In the first phase, two physicians will approve every AI-generated prescription before it’s sent to the user. Once this has been done for at least 100 patients, and if there are no serious problems, it will then progress to stage two, where the AI issues the prescriptions directly without any human approval, and physicians review them after the fact. This stage will cover 500 patients, Nolla Health said.
Finally, in stage three, human physicians will simply review at least 10% of all automated prescriptions made by Nolla on a monthly basis. The pilot project is being launched as part of Utah’s AI Learning Lab sandbox program, which provides AI firms with relief from state laws to test new products under supervision. “Taking part in our AI sandbox does not mean the State of Utah has approved, endorsed, certified, or vouched for the product,” the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy states on its authorized-pilots page.
Acne as a proof-of-concept
In an interview with Inc.com, Nolla Health Chief Medical Adviser Zaid Fadul said that acne treatment is only the starting point. The startup has much bigger ambitions in future, he said. If the pilot is successful, it will then look at bringing automated prescription services to other common conditions that are well-understood by doctors, simple to assess remotely and can be treated using medications with strong safety profiles.
“Beyond dermatology, I think conditions like the flu and uncomplicated urinary tract infections are worth exploring, particularly because testing can provide objective information that can be considered alongside a patient’s symptoms and medical history,” Fadul said. “The key is having very clear guardrails.”
Ten years from now, Fadul said, he expects that AI will be able to manage a large part of routine human healthcare checks, including diagnostics, treatments, prescription refills and routine testing. But he doesn’t foresee AI being used when it comes to more serious medical conditions and life-changing diagnoses, or with major procedures and high-risk medications.
Some medications, such as stimulants, opioids and benzodiazepines are too risky for AI to prescribe, he said, given the risk that some humans might try to manipulate the models doing the assessments. “Frankly, it may take a long time before we have enough evidence and the appropriate safeguards to support autonomous prescribing of some of these drugs,” Fadul said.

articles.title: Google limita la versión gratuita de Gemini a Flash-Lite 3.5 y AI Plus a Flash 3.6
articles.text:
Google limitará el acceso gratuito a Gemini desde el 9 de octubre de 2026: los usuarios sin suscripción solo podrán utilizar Gemini Flash-Lite 3.5, mientras que el plan AI Plus habilitará Gemini Flash 3.6. La medida reorganiza el acceso a los modelos según el nivel de pago y el consumo de recursos informáticos de cada tarea.
El cambio profundiza el sistema que la compañía introdujo en mayo de 2026, cuando dejó de aplicar un número fijo de mensajes y pasó a calcular los límites según la capacidad de procesamiento requerida por cada consulta.
Google detalló en su página de soporte que la implementación comenzará en los próximos días. Alcanzará tanto a quienes usan la aplicación sin costo como a los suscriptores de sus planes de inteligencia artificial (IA).
Cómo quedará el acceso a la inteligencia artificial en cada plan de Google
Los usuarios gratuitos perderán el acceso a Gemini Flash y Gemini Pro. Su única alternativa será Gemini Flash-Lite 3.5, un modelo pensado para respuestas rápidas y tareas de menor complejidad.
Por su parte, el plan Google AI Plus, disponible en España por 4,99 euros mensuales, permitirá utilizar Flash-Lite 3.5 y Flash 3.6. Sin embargo, sus suscriptores tampoco tendrán acceso al modelo Pro.
Los planes Google AI Pro y AI Ultra concentrarán el acceso más amplio. Por 21,99 euros y 99,99 euros al mes, respectivamente, sus usuarios podrán usar todos los modelos disponibles, incluida la versión Gemini Pro 3.1.
Además, los abonados a AI Pro y AI Ultra podrán usar Deep Think en la aplicación de Gemini. Esta opción permite emplear el máximo nivel de razonamiento paralelo del modelo y hasta ahora estaba reservada al nivel Ultra.
Para qué es útil cada modelo de inteligencia artificial de Google
Gemini Flash-Lite está orientado a consultas directas que requieren rapidez y un menor consumo de recursos. Puede responder preguntas breves, traducir textos cortos, resumir contenidos o clasificar datos en una fracción de segundo.
En cambio, Gemini Flash está diseñado para problemas que exigen analizar varios pasos de forma simultánea. Sus aplicaciones incluyen la evaluación de situaciones complejas, la escritura o corrección de código y la coordinación de tareas consecutivas.
La diferencia entre ambos modelos dependerá de la necesidad del usuario: Flash-Lite prioriza la velocidad y el menor costo operativo, mientras que Flash busca ofrecer respuestas más elaboradas ante consultas que requieren mayor análisis.
Asimismo, Google permitirá elegir el nivel de esfuerzo para cada tarea en los modelos disponibles: bajo, medio o alto. La opción más alta incrementa la capacidad del sistema para completar solicitudes y elaborar respuestas más exhaustivas, aunque consume una porción mayor del límite de procesamiento.
La compañía no precisó cómo incorporará Gemini 4 Argon, presentado el 1 de octubre de 2026. El nuevo modelo se desplegará inicialmente entre defensores cibernéticos a través del programa Fairwind.
Qué es todo lo se sabe de Gemini 4 Argon de Google
Gemini 4 Argon fue desarrollado por Alphabet a través de Google DeepMind para programación, investigación, redacción y trabajo profesional, con énfasis en la ciberseguridad. La compañía lo presentó como el modelo más avanzado de su catálogo hasta el momento.
El acceso no estará disponible de inmediato para usuarios finales. Google DeepMind priorizará a administraciones públicas, centros de salud y servicios de telecomunicaciones, con el objetivo de que los grupos de trabajo que desarrollan defensas informáticas empleen la herramienta antes de que capacidades similares puedan utilizarse contra diferentes sistemas digitales.
La compañía dijo que Argon puede “encontrar, validar y corregir de forma autónoma vulnerabilidades críticas de software”. Esa facultad explica que su lanzamiento inicial se concentre en socios especializados en seguridad informática.
La iniciativa valida los hallazgos y los comunica de forma privada a las organizaciones afectadas, con prioridad para hospitales, servicios públicos e infraestructuras esenciales. Los problemas más frecuentes identificados por ese programa están relacionados con fallas de autorización y con la exposición de credenciales.

- Cops criticized for using Flock to stop a woman without probable cause
- Judge says searches based on Flock breach the Fourth Amendment
Flock cameras represent “indiscriminate mass surveillance” and should be ruled unconstitutional, a federal judge has just declared. It’s yet another blow to the beleaguered automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) camera maker and reflects growing public opposition to the technology.
The declaration was made when Oklahoma judge Sara Hill ruled that a police officer had violated the Fourth Amendment rights of a woman suspected of methamphetamine trafficking by searching for her license plate in Flock’s database.
According to 404 Media, the police officer looked up the license plate simply because it was from California, then used the woman’s travel history as justification for searching her car. In other words, he worked backwards after finding the woman’s vehicle in the Flock database instead of relying on any kind of probable cause.
The Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution protects citizens against “unreasonable searches and seizures.” In this instance, the judge ruled that Flock’s network of cameras was “a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that had been harnessed by the officer. The judge’s reasoning was that the license plate search “was not supported by probable cause, and it was done without a warrant in violation of [the defendant’s] Fourth Amendment rights.”
Hill disagreed with previous judicial opinions that Flock’s network did not breach the Fourth Amendment because its footage was taken in public places. They argued that these opinions do not consider that the network is “approaching dragnet-type law enforcement practice” and that courts need to catch up to keep abreast of the technology.
Flock’s ‘sweeping modes of surveillance’
In the case in question, the police officer got lucky when he pulled over the woman: she was in fact carrying 91 pounds of methamphetamine in her vehicle. But his motivation for pulling her over was the problem: she was simply driving in Oklahoma using a car with California license plates. That was not enough of a “probable cause” to justify the traffic stop, the judge ruled, and constituted a violation of the woman’s Fourth Amendment rights against arbitrary searches.
As the judge argued, “The factors that the government relies upon are the same type of circumstances that everyday Americans encounter on long road trips for many legitimate reasons. Many of us drive longer than we want to get to a desired destination, or to no destination at all other than the road and sights ahead.” Using Flock’s catalog of vehicle footage to stop these everyday people would infringe on their Constitutional rights, Hill declared.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
404 Media believes there are currently over 100,000 warrantless license plate searches made within Flock’s systems every month. Hill’s decision is not binding, but it comes shortly after a similar decision ruled that traffic stops made by the US Border Patrol using data from ALPR cameras were unconstitutional.
As Michael Soyfer, a lawyer at the Institute for Justice, put it, Hill’s decision recognizes “the sheer breadth of these systems, that they collect so much information about so many people in a way that sets them apart … The way courts have resolved these cases previously has been way too myopic and has ignored the depths of these systems and the sweeping modes of surveillance that allow police to reconstruct the movements of anyone in the country.”
We don’t know whether this ruling and others like it will lead to any significant changes, and as noted, previous cases have decided that Flock cameras do not present a Fourth Amendment risk. But with public opinion solidifying against the cameras and law enforcement’s reliance on the tech increasingly called into question, it’s an issue that will likely continue to face scrutiny going forward.

articles.title: The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It
articles.text:
Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI, all connect to data, services, and each other securely. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, because organizations first need to understand what credentials exist, where they live, and what they can access. This is the first of three articles we are releasing that explain the reason behind our mission.
—
Software production is accelerating beyond the growth assumptions that shaped many of today's security controls. GitHub COO Kyle Daigle said the platform had gone from roughly 1 billion commits during all of 2025 to 2.9 billion commits in August 2026, an annualized pace of over 14 billion for the 2026 reporting year. GitHub's own engineering team has gone further in its capacity planning, saying it moved from preparing for 10x scale to designing for a future that requires 30x today's scale as agentic development accelerated.
All of this code prodiction means more infrastructure and more secrets. More applications, new types of integrations, automations, and now agents, mean more systems need to authenticate to something else. Credential exposure has already been a problem of increasing scale. GitGuardian detected 28.65 million new hardcoded secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, up 34% year over year. Leaked credentials associated with AI services increased 81%.
Security teams need to establish visibility into that expanding credential layer right now.
GitGuardian approaches credential-layer security through three connected stages: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. Detection comes first because every action that follows depends on knowing which credentials actually exist, where they have spread, and what access they represent.
The credential layer has no convenient perimeter
The credential layer is the collection of credentials connecting people, applications, infrastructure, and services across an enterprise.
Its perimeter follows the credentials themselves.
A developer will create a secret inside a sanctioned cloud account and later that same key, in plaintext, will appear in a repository or in a shared knowledgebase. Other secrets will be stored in an approved vault while a plaintext copies remain on the developer's laptop. More may be created outside security's normal vantage point through a personal project or a newly adopted AI service, especially by an increasingly growing number fo 'citizen developers' who now have access to coding agents.
The result is an attack surface that crosses all technology and ownership boundaries.
The same GitGuardian State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research we referenced earlier shows how wide this surface has become. Internal repositories were roughly six times more likely than public repositories to contain at least one secret. Around 28% of secrets incidents originated entirely outside source-code repositories in collaboration and productivity systems.
That leaves security teams with a basic discovery challenge. Each scanner, vault, repository, or endpoint can describe the part of the credential layer it sees. The organization still needs a way to understand the combined population.
Every discovery source provides a partial picture
Source control remains essential because hardcoded credentials leave durable evidence.
A credential removed from the current version of a file can remain in Git history. Copies can spread into other branches or repositories. Public exposure can put the value beyond the organization's control, making it extremely challenging for anyone to immediately notice.
Internal repositories reveal another large population. They contain the credentials developers and applications use during normal work, including access to cloud environments and internal services.
Collaboration systems expose a different part of the credential layer. Credentials get pasted into tickets while troubleshooting. They move through chat during handoffs. They can remain searchable long after the work that required them is finished.
Developer laptops are holding all the credentials
Developers are at the heart of all of this creation, use and placement of secrets. Until recently it was considered normal form to use local local environment files to hold application secrets using command-line tools cache credentials used to reach cloud services. The danger of an unscrubbed local shell history, which can preserve values long after someone has forgotten they were entered, seemed rather low.
Then the attackers shifted. The end of 2025 brought new waves of infostealer attacks like Shai-Hulud and S1ingularity, which turned the developer laptop into a target and an entry point into the supply chain.
Every laptop is part of the credential layer and the secrets they hold need to be mapped.
Repository scanning shows credentials that reached source control. Public monitoring reveals exposures outside corporate repositories. Endpoint discovery identifies secrets that may never have entered a centrally monitored system.
The credential layer only becomes visible when those perspectives are connected.
Attackers already search across those boundaries
Attackers have already adapted to the fact that credentials exist across managed and unmanaged environments.
Compromised credentials already accounted for 22% of initial access according to the the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report. Their data also found corporate credentials on unmanaged devices, which drove a significant number of the breaches they researched. Enterprise access can quickly cross a boundary that security teams consider meaningful.
And their data reporting period ended before the information stealer worms became as wide spread as we saw in early 2026.
This self propagating malware running on an endpoint can search browser data, local files, and application storage. It can collect whatever authentication material is available without caring which team created it or which security product was supposed to govern it.
Developer systems offer an especially valuable targets. A developer machine may authenticate to source control and cloud infrastructure. It can also hold local credentials for applications under development. Compromising that endpoint can expose access that spans several otherwise separate parts of the enterprise.
Security teams need to perform that inventory before an attacker does.
The developer laptop is being shared with a new type of user
The developer endpoint has always accumulated credentials because building software requires connecting systems. But now there is a new type of internal actor that has access to that same machine, AI agents.
Coding agents can read files, execute commands, and interact with external services. Model Context Protocol connections can give those agents access to additional tools. Each connection introduces another place where authentication and authorization need to be established.
GitGuardian's analysis of systems compromised during the Shai-Hulud 2 supply-chain campaign provides a rare view into the density of credentials on these machines. Across 6,943 compromised systems, researchers identified 33,185 unique secrets. Forty-four percent of compromised machines held more than 10 secrets, while 5% contained more than 100.
At the same time, how we are authenticating AI agents have introduced a new security hole. In the same report we saw 24,008 unique secrets in public MCP configuration files during 2025, of which, 2,117 could be verified as valid.
A security team that scans repositories can know a great deal about repositories. It still has limited visibility into credentials living on the machines where code is created, tested, and connected to external systems.
AI agents can do unexpected things with this access. It can be abused by attackers, but just as likely it can result in negative outcomes from the AI taking a surprising move, like deleting a production database.
Security teams need to understand what exactly these agents can access to understand the risk.
Discovery needs context around every credential
Finding a secret provides the first coordinate. Security teams need the surrounding context to understand the risk it represents.
Validity is one of the most immediate signals.
Unfortunately, most secrets stay valid far longer than they should. Ideally, any credential would be made just in time, and expire after use, but GitGuardian retested credentials that had been confirmed valid in 2022 and found that 64% were still valid in January 2026.
A credential can therefore remain useful to an attacker years after the original exposure.
A secret's location adds another dimension to risk assessment.
A credential found once in an internal repository has one exposure history. The same credential appearing on a laptop and later in a public repository has traveled much farther. Every occurrence expands the set of people and systems that may have had access to it.
Credential fingerprinting can connect those appearances while preserving a single credential record. Seven detections of the same secret represent one credential with seven known exposures. Treating it that way produces a more accurate inventory and a clearer picture of how far it has spread.
Ownership provides another layer.
Security teams need to know which user, workload, or application relies on the credential. Ownership connects the finding to the team responsible for managing the access, not just who created it, but what policy or governance does this fall under.
The scope of permissions shows what the credential can do and the danger it brings.
A credential limited to a development service presents one scope of risk. A production credential with broad administrative permissions presents another. Validity and permission context together reveal which findings deserve the fastest attention.
Dependencies complete more of the picture.
A credential can be highly exposed while still supporting critical workloads. Understanding those relationships gives the organization the information it will eventually need to rotate or revoke the credential safely.
Discovery should produce a credential record enriched with this context.
Security teams need a real denominator for their coverage metrics
Many enterprises already have strong secrets-management programs.
Those systems provide valuable information about credentials already under management. They can show what is stored, who has access, and how the secret is being used.
The larger credential layer mapping determines how complete that coverage really is.
For example, a company might have 50,000 credentials stored in approved vaults while thousands more sit in plaintext in repositories, developer endpoints, or collaboration systems. But from their reporting, they show how the secrets they know about are accounted for, blind to the ones created outside of their planned paved paths. Some of those credentials may correspond to values already held in the vault. Others may exist completely outside any approved manager.
Security teams need to know how much of the credential population has an identified owner. They need to know how many active credentials can be connected to permissions and dependent workloads. They also need visibility into which credentials have crossed into public environments.
Those measurements depend on discovering the population first.
Everything is speeding up, including attackers
Security programs built around periodic discovery will face increasing pressure as software production accelerates. This historic growth represents more than additional code.
GitGuardian's reports show, that over the time they have been researching this area, secret exposure has increased 1.6 times faster than the number of active developers.
Attackers are leveraging this while also accelerating their attack speeds.
CrowdStrike reported an average eCrime breakout time of 29 minutes in 2025, with the fastest observed case reaching lateral movement in 27 seconds. Defenders need to react in terms of machine speed, as the days of a human executing an attack are now past us. The time available to respond will only continue to shrink.
The answer can not just be faster reaction, but a shift towards prevention. And that is not possible until you understand what you are trying to prevent, which in turn requires knowledge of what is surfaces you currently even have for credentials to leak into.
Detection builds the map for everything that follows
The first step in controlling credential risk is understanding the credential layer the organization actually has.
That requires discovery across repositories, public exposure, and developer endpoints. It also requires context around every credential, including validity, ownership, permissions, and dependencies.
Vault coverage becomes one measurement inside that larger picture. Repository findings become another. Endpoint discoveries add credentials that may have remained invisible to central security systems.
Together, they create a usable inventory of the credential layer.
The approach of "detect, remediate, and prevent" starts with that inventory because remediation and prevention depend on it. Security teams need to know what exists before they can systematically remove risky credentials or stop new exposure from spreading.
The growth already underway raises the cost of waiting.
GitHub's move from 1 billion annual commits to a pace measured in hundreds of millions per week provides a glimpse of the software volume ahead. GitHub itself is preparing infrastructure for a future measured at 30 times today's scale. Every new application, agent, and integration can extend the credential layer further.
Security teams need visibility capable of expanding at the same pace.

articles.title: À 10 000 €, elle va tout casser : Citroën ressuscite la mythique 2CV en version électrique
articles.text:
L’une des voitures françaises les plus célèbres au monde s’apprête à faire un retour en fanfare. La Citroën 2CV revient en effet au XXIème siècle sous une forme électrique qui entend une nouvelle fois révolutionner le marché. Le constructeur vise en effet un prix ultra bas qui pourrait tutoyer les 10 000 € aides comprises, ce qui ferait de l’auto la voiture électrique la moins chère d’Europe, tout simplement.
En attendant une présentation officielle le 11 octobre, Citroën fait monter la température avec les premières images de ce concept car prometteur. On y remarque par exemple un feu semi-circulaire mordu sur deux côtés. L’ensemble évasé rappelle bien entendu les optiques rondes de la 2CV originale plantés sur les ailes. L’histoire se répète sur le capot bombé orné de stries comme sur l’ancêtre. Une signature que l’on pourrait retrouver en série.
Des clins d’œil rétro qui font mouche
Ce qui a également toutes ses chances de passer en production sont les jantes au look éminemment rétro. Pleines avec quatre écrous au lieu de trois, elles se voient chaussées de pneus Michelin arborant la police d’écriture des années 1950. Un sympathique clin d’œil, qui s’accompagne de flancs bas garnis de chevrons indiquant le sens de rotation du pneumatique. On remarquera aussi des passages de roues noirs brillants.
Dépourvu de vitre, le montant C montre pour sa part un feu de position orange tiré droit de la première 2CV. Pivotantes, les poignées de portes devraient loger sur des portières avant à charnières inversées comme sur le modèle original. Peu de chance en revanche qu’un tel système soit repris sur la version de série en raison des coûts de développement supérieurs. Car là est toute la philosophie de cette réinterprétation.
Le pari fou du low-cost : comment Citroën casse les prix
L’auto devra être extrêmement compétitive à l’instar de son ancêtre en contenant sévèrement ses prix. Citroën vise un tarif de 15 000 € sans aides, ce qui est bien en deçà de la ë-C3. Avec la Prime Coup de Pouce maximale, la facture devrait alors atteindre les 10 000 €, ce qui serait tout bonnement imbattable sur le marché, toutes catégories confondues. Alléchant, même s’il faudra forcément faire quelques compromis.
L’autonomie devrait être limitée par une batterie des plus compactes. Le pack de 30 kWh de la ë-C3 en version Autonomie Urbaine sera le candidat pressenti. Le rayon d’action tournera alors autour des 200 km sur le cycle WLTP. La puissance sera aussi bien modeste en passant sous les 100 ch, alors que la recharge rapide figurera en option. Rendez-vous la semaine prochaine pour tout savoir sur ce concept qui entrera en production en 2028 !

articles.title: Qualcomm Licenses Huawei's LogicFolding, 5G, and Other Technologies
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 6th 2026
Qualcomm Licenses Huawei's LogicFolding, 5G, and Other Technologies
Qualcomm announced today that it is officially licensing technology from Chinese technology giant Huawei. In a deal estimated to be worth $6.9 billion upon completion, Qualcomm will license various technologies from Huawei to integrate across its product portfolio. According to official releases, these technologies include computing, AI, networking, and more. Bloomberg reports that the deal also covers Huawei's latest LogicFolding silicon design. This is a significant win for Huawei, whose R&D teams have spent years designing a way to bypass sanctions and overcome manufacturing technology limits. By stacking silicon vertically across two sheets, LogicFolding dramatically reduces the distance between compute elements, increases efficiency, and significantly improves transistor density. The result is a 55% increase in transistor density and a 41% boost in power efficiency.
Update, 06:30 UTC, October 6: Qualcomm issued a statement that dismantles rumors that the company is licensing LogicFolding technology.
QualcommQualcomm and Huawei entered into a multi-year, broad patent license agreement that includes cross-licenses across a range of technology fields. The terms are confidential, but reports characterizing Qualcomm as a net payor on the license agreement are incorrect. In addition, assertions that the agreement is related to LogicFold are not accurate. Separately, Qualcomm has agreed to purchase certain Huawei non-cellular U.S. patents across multiple technology areas.
Since Huawei lacks access to manufacturing its silicon using EUV lithography, it uses DUV machines with LogicFolding to work around this limitation. Even so, the company claims that LogicFolding on its domestic node production will achieve a transistor density equivalent to a 1.4 nm node by 2031. For Qualcomm, whose access to advanced lithography is unrestricted, this means the company can potentially surpass Moore's Law by stacking multiple sheets of cutting-edge silicon, achieving massive boosts in transistor density and power efficiency.
This agreement will be completed after regulatory approvals are secured. Huawei sees it as a way to collaborate with the industry and share its technology under fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) principles. For other technologies, Huawei's development and contributions to 4G and 5G standards are so advanced that they lead in some areas, such as near-physical-limit signal transmission technology using polar codes. Qualcomm will utilize these technologies in building its own modems and designs, selecting only what best suits its use cases.

articles.title: Signed data pioneer SignSplit launches with $400M to help everyone get paid for their AI contributions - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Signed data pioneer SignSplit launches with $400M to help everyone get paid for their AI contributions
Few technology companies can help users to protect and monetize their personal data for artificial intelligence as well as SignSplit PBC, it seems.
That explains why it has already secured a massive $1 billion valuation today after launching with a bumper $400 million in funding from W Group, a global group consisting of 11 financial technology firms focused on blockchain tech. SignSplit was quietly established back in 2024, with its founders setting out to resolve the growing challenge around personal data and provenance at a time when AI was getting thirstier than ever for information.
The startup, led by co-founder and Chief Executive Alessandro Monterosso, believes that the next generation of AI and intelligent robotics is going to need extremely high-quality, real-world human data, knowledge and creativity across fields spanning science, media and healthcare. However, most existing AI models make do with data that’s scraped from the internet, and that much of it has opaque origins.
To obtain access to higher quality human data, AI developers will likely have to pay for it, and that means having a system in place to establish clear provenance, permissions and usage rights. This is where SplitSign’s concept of “signed data” comes into play.
Signed data refers to human data contributions that have established provenance and give clear consent for it to be used under defined terms. It has built the underlying infrastructure that enables this signed data to be contributed, verified, protected and licensed, ensuring that anyone who provides high-quality data will be compensated for doing so.
For individual contributors, SignSplit offers a clear promise: They simply “sign the data and split the value.” Users can protect their digital assets, including specific datasets, their likeness, their voices and other bodies of work, by digitally signing them to establish verifiable consent and the terms under which that data can be used by AI models.
Alternatively, users can contribute their data into what SignSplit calls “data pools,” which aggregate very specific types of data from multiple users and make it available to AI developers. The more value their data creates, the greater the financial upside for the contributors, who are compensated based on how often it’s used.
Monterosso said the boundary between technology and human experience is becoming increasingly blurred. “As AI reaches further into the real world, human knowledge, creativity, skills and identity will become increasingly connected to how technology evolves and interacts with the world around us,” he said. “We believe SignSplit and the use of signed data can become the bridge between the two, connecting human contribution with protection, participation and compensation as technology advances.”
Though SignSplit wants individual humans to contribute their data and get paid for it, it’s also targeting companies with the offer of access to the exact type of high-quality datasets they need, without any legal concerns or ethical ambiguity. Businesses can create their own data pools and define what kind of real-world data or skills they need to train their AI models, allowing individuals to contribute it to them directly, so long as they agree to the terms requested by the company.
There are also “research pools” specifically for universities and life sciences firms, heard towards one-off and ongoing studies that require real human participation. Organizations can also use SignSplit’s verification layer to check if a specific dataset or likeness is signed, so they can ensure their intended use meets the conditions associated with it.
W Group founder and President Volodymyr Nosov said his group will devote additional capital and resources to accelerate a rapid global rollout of SignSplit’s technology, aiding its push to become the founding infrastructure of AI’s emerging signed-data economy.
“SignedSplit sets a new standard for the use of individuals’ and institutions’ data, work and likenesses,” he said. “We believe that every serious participant in AI and the data economy will come to rely on SignSplit’s infrastructure, and the scale of our commitment reflects both how early we believe we are, and how important we believe these solutions will be for every industry that relies on human data.”

articles.title: GPT-6 Astra se cansó de perder en StarCraft. Lo que hizo para ganar sorprendió hasta a los organizadores del torneo
articles.text:
Llevamos años poniendo a modelos de IA a jugar a videojuegos para medir sus capacidades y en eso precisamente consiste StarSkirmish, un torneo creado por aficionados a 'StarCraft: Brood War' en el que se enfrentan varios modelos de IA. GPT-6 Astra era uno de los participantes, pero no dejaba de acumular derrotas, así que tomó una decisión tan efectiva como tramposa.
El objetivo. Lo cuentan en el portal Kotaku. Durante la última edición de este torneo competían GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 y Pluto, un bot desarrollado por un aficionado. Los modelos tenían una hora para programar un bot capaz de controlar la facción Protoss en 'StarCraft: Brood War'. Ese bot debía encargarse de recolectar recursos, construir edificios y unidades y tomar decisiones tácticas durante las partidas. Es decir, que la prueba no consistía en que la IA jugara directamente, sino en que generara el programa que tomaba todas las decisiones dentro del juego.
La trampa. GPT-6 Astra perdía de forma habitual frente a sus oponentes. En lugar de mejorar su programación, el modelo tomó otra dirección: decidió descargarse Stardust, un bot al que el creador del torneo, Kai McPheeters, calificó como "el bot de StarCraft escrito por humanos con la calificación #1 según los rankings BASIL". Es decir, que GPT-6 Astra dedujo que el método óptimo para alzarse con la victoria consistía en emplear un bot ajeno con eficacia demostrada en combate. McPheeters descartó el código de Astra para evitar que quedara "contaminado" por la trampa y asegura que el modelo ya es capaz de superar a bots de divisiones superiores.
Antecedentes. Aunque el intento pueda parecer anecdótico, los modelos de OpenAI ya han sido sorprendidos haciendo trampas en numerosas ocasiones y no es algo que haya empezado ahora. Hace casi una década, un modelo temprano de IA aprovechó fallos y vulnerabilidades del juego para arañar segundos en Sonic the Hedgehog. Este tipo de comportamientos llevan años siendo estudiados por los investigadores y reciben el nombre de 'Reward Hacking'. Para entenderlo de forma más simple, es como si te dan como objetivo aprobar un examen y, en lugar de estudiar, te las apañas para robar las respuestas.
El caso Hugging Face. Es quizás el incidente más grave que se ha registrado. Este verano, OpenAI hizo público que, durante prueba de seguridad, un modelo experimental aprovechó una brecha para salir de su entorno aislado y después accedió a los repositorios de Hugging Face en busca de la respuesta al reto planteado. Después supimos que el ataque fue llevado a cabo por 700 agentes de IA, los cuales se organizaron para lograr un objetivo común.
Aquel incidente fue el que encendió la mecha del debate sobre los riesgos de una IA fuera de control. De hecho, OpenAI afronta una demanda interpuesta por una organización jurídica sin ánimo de lucro que busca depurar responsabilidades por las conductas autónomas de sus modelos.
