articles.title: Data centers to factory floors: Walden robots learn on the job - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Physical AI’s bottleneck shifts from what robots can do to whether factories trust them
AI is moving beyond the data centers where models are trained and onto factory floors where machines must handle constant change.
But traditional industrial robots work behind a cage, repeat a single task and were never designed for the complexities of today’s market. Manufacturers now want general-purpose machines that can switch tasks and improve as processes evolve. The hard part is deploying it, according to Adrien Gaidon (pictured, right), co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics Inc.
“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon said. “What we do is we do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”
Gaidon and John Mancuso (left), vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante at Fully Connected, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cloud infrastructure, simulation and human assistance help robots learn and adapt on factory floors. (* Disclosure below.)
Physical AI moves from data centers to the factory floor
Walden spun out of Toyota Research Institute in January 2026 and launched with $300 million in July to put general-purpose robots to work in manufacturing. Its robots have worked full production shifts alongside people since May. They handle machine tending, parts kitting, and subassembly, tasks manufacturers had either failed to automate or never tried, Gaidon explained.
“There’s half a million open positions for machinists in the U.S. because it’s a hard job and it requires skills,” Gaidon said. “But part of that job does not require the craft or the human creativity.”
Getting a robot to that point takes serious compute long before it reaches a production line. CoreWeave, which has been betting on physical AI, also brings mechanical engineers and robotics experts into customer engagements alongside its infrastructure, Mancuso explained.
“In the end, before a model is ever going to do something in the physical world, it’s going to have a tremendous amount of simulation that happens in the virtual world,” Mancuso said. “We’re providing the infrastructure.”
But while simulation in data centers can make a robot useful, but it can’t make it perfect. Walden pairs autonomous robots with remote human assistants. The setup is comparable to automated looms of 120 years ago, when one person oversaw 40 machines, Gaidon noted.
“Our robots are autonomous, but they know how to call for help,” Gaidon said. “They know when they need some assistance – and that assistance feeds the most valuable data to improve over time.”

articles.title: FashionTech startup Rodinia Generation aims to save 100 billion litres of water annually, secures €4 million | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Danish FashionTech startup Rodinia Generation, a developer of clothing production technology, has raised €4 million to finance their industrial phase, including the establishment of a first commercial-scale facility in Portugal, planned for 2027.
The round was led by Vitamin°C, with continued backing from existing investors Climentum Capital and EIFO. This follows a €3 million raise in 2024, as reported by EU-Startups.
“Manufacturing closer to demand has never been more strategically valuable than it is right now,” says Trine Young, founder and CEO of Rodinia Generation. “The brands that produce with us have no need to predict what will sell months in advance. They also don’t need to produce at high volumes to reach better unit economics. They can react to demand in days instead of months, sell more at full price and manage inventory and cash much more efficiently – and on top of all this, they can do so with a much lower environmental footprint.”
Rodinia Generation’s financing comes amid continued European investment in technologies addressing the environmental and manufacturing footprint of textiles and apparel.
In 2026, EU-Startups has reported rounds including €5 million for fellow Copenhagen-based Octarine Bio to industrialise its sustainable pigment platform, €4.2 million for Cambridge-based Sparxell’s plant-based colour technology, €10.3 million for London-based Epoch Biodesign to commercialise textile and nylon recycling, €300k for Malmö-based Salt & Fiber’s seagrass-derived textile fibres, and €26.1 million for Paris-based Syntetica to build a commercial demonstration facility for nylon recycling.
Together with Bristol-based Ponda’s €1.6 million Seed extension, these comparable rounds amount to approximately €47.5 million, rising to around €51.5 million when Rodinia’s latest financing is included.
Lead investor Vitamin°C and existing backer Climentum Capital have also been active in 2026 after announcing first closes of €18 million and €60 million respectively for their climate-focused funds.
“Rodinia is tackling one of the largest industries in the world with a fundamentally different manufacturing model. What attracted us is not sustainability alone, but the potential to change the economics of apparel production by combining automation, flexi bility and local manufacturing at commercial scale,” adds Nathalie Moral, Founding Partner at Vitamin°C.
Founded in 2017, Rodinia Generation operates out of Copenhagen, Denmark and is a technology company founded by entrepreneur Trine Young.
In 2021 the pilot O-Factory opened in Copenhagen demonstrating a new garment production system built on three technology pillars: proprietary software, proprietary machinery, and the ability to selectively integrate external technologies and make them economically useful at industrial scale.
The Copenhagen facility has produced for fashion brands since 2021 and is currently producing the next collections for Henrik Vibskov and Klaus Samsøe.
“We have demonstrated in Copenhagen that a single O-factory line can produce 80% of clothing categories, including evening dresses, formal shirts, football tees, swimwear and childrenswear, just to mention a few of the categories that have already achieved competitive margins. The investment allows Rodinia to increase production capacity for existing and new brands with the opening of our industrial-scale O-factory in Portugal,” says Trine.
According to the company, fashion production is becoming increasingly difficult to automate because the industry no longer simply manufactures large quantities of identical products. Today brands need the flexibility to produce thousands of styles, allow for frequent product changes and achieve increasingly shorter production runs at competitive unit economics.
Rodinia’s O-factory is built for this complexity. The technology combines proprietary software and machinery with selected external production technologies, allowing production settings to adapt as the digital input of each garment changes.
Rodinia’s longer-term ambition is a global network of O-factories located closer to the major markets of fashion brands.
“By replicating flexible production capacity across different locations, we are creating the foundation for a new manufacturing infrastructure for the global apparel industry,” adds Trine.
The O-factory is designed to reduce CO₂e emissions by approximately 40% per average garment while eliminating water use from its production process.
Based on Rodinia’s current impact calculations, when O-factories are producing the equivalent of just half the annual garment volume of a large fast-fashion brand, approximately 100 billion litres of water and one million tonnes of CO₂e will be saved every year compared with conventional production.

articles.title: Tom Cruise se estrella en taquilla con 'Digger', uno de los peores estrenos de toda su carrera: las pérdidas serán millonarias
articles.text:
Tom Cruise volvía este pasado fin de semana a los cines con su nueva y esperadísima película, Digger. Dirigida por el prestigioso director Alejandro G. Iñárritu, el filme apuntaba a ser uno de los posibles grandes lanzamientos de la temporada otoñal. Sin embargo, los resultados han sido radicalmente opuestos a los que actor y cineasta podías esperar. Porque ya no hay duda, el proyecto es un fracaso rotundo.
Y es que, tal y como se ha desvelado, Digger tan solo ha recaudado 8 millones de dólares en la taquilla estadounidense y otros 12 millones en el resto del mundo, sumando un estreno de apenas 20 millones de dólares. Se trata del peor estreno de Tom Cruise en los últimos 19 años, desde Leones por corderos allá por 2007.
Si tenemos en cuenta que, además, Digger ha costado 160 millones de dólares, la película se confirma como uno de los mayores fracasos de toda su carrera. Un doloroso varapalo para un actor que acostumbra a llenar los cines sencillamente con su estatus de estrella, como demuestran las sagas Top Gun y Misión Imposible. Por desgracia, esta vez Tom Cruise no ha sabido conectar con el público, que no ha respondido ni a nivel económico ni en las valoraciones, pues el filme cuenta con una triste puntuación de C+ en CinemaScore.
Las pérdidas millonarias de Digger
Tal y como recoge Deadline en un nuevo reporte, los datos de taquilla de Digger son algo realmente preocupante. La película se enfrentaría a unas pérdidas de hasta 150 millones de dólares. Y eso en el escenario relativamente optimista de que al menos alcance los 50 millones de recaudación total. Algo que ni siquiera está claro que vaya a suceder. Estrenos recientes anteriores como Smashing Machine (2025) o Amsterdam (2022) tuvieron estrenos similares y su taquilla total apenas llegó a los 21 y 31 millones, respectivamente.
Con el desastre de Digger, Tom Cruise sigue profundizando en la herida de lo que se ha convertido en un año muy difícil para Warner Bros. El estudio, que tuvo un 2025 brillante y que acaba de ser comprado por Paramount Skydance, ha encadenado varias películas este curso que han rendido por debajo de lo esperado: Cumbres borrascosas, ¡La Novia!, Te van a matar, La Momia de Lee Cronin, Mortal Kombat II, Supergirl, Evil Dead Burn, El final de Oak Street y Prácticamente Magia 2.
Digger de Tom Cruise se suma ahora a esta lista de películas con el mayor fracaso de todos. Una superproducción de este nivel de ambición debería haber optado a números sobresalientes en taquilla, así como una buena carrera de premios y nominaciones. Pero no está siendo el año de Warner Bros., a la que aún le queda la esperanzadora bala de Dune 3 en diciembre. Eso sí, tendrá que competir con un coloso como Avengers: Doomsday, que se estrena el mismo día.

articles.title: Apple's new M6 Mac mini drops $120 for October Prime Day
articles.text:
Apple's new M6 Mac mini just got a $120 price drop ahead of Prime Big Deal Days
Apple's new Mac mini computer just got its first price cut ahead of Amazon Big Deal Days
What's the deal?
Apple's new Mac mini desktop computer is down to $799.99, a saving of almost $120 (or 13%) off its official selling price. It is very rare for Apple to drop the price of a popular product that quickly and that deeply after launch.
Grab that "Big Day Deals" special as it won't be around for long. Amazon says that more than 2,000 in the past month have been sold, no surprise that it is the best seller in mini PCs there.
The 2026 model of the ever-popular Apple Mac mini desktop gets its first price cut since launch.
In the UK: now £824 (was £899)
What is it?
This is the newest evolution of the Mac mini. This 2026 version of the award winning, game changing tiny PC crams a lot of new technology into a familiar form factor and that makes it higher price tag more palatable. There's Wi-Fi 7, now powered by Apple's own wireless chip, and standard 2.5Gb LAN ports but the cherry on the cake is the new mighty M6 chip. 0
According to two respected test sites (CPUBenchmark and GeekBench), it is the fastest single thread processor ever produce, ahead of the M5 Ultra. Let that sink down for a second. Apple's cheapest PC is powered by a blindingly quick processor with a solid penchant for AI workloads. You don't see that in the world of AMD and Intel.
Other than the 12-core CPU, the M6 has a 12-core GPU and two 16-core Neural Engine NPU to tackle those all important 'personal, professional and creative tasks'. The onboard memory (16GB) and SSD (256GB) are the two major letdowns but then again, that's against the backdrop of the ongoing RAMpocalypse that decimated global memory and NAND markets. On the other hand it is the only mini PC in this price range with three Thunderbolt 4 ports.
What others say?
The Guardian (5/5): “Truly mighty but now more pricey… Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse.”
Wired (4.5/5): “Apple has refreshed the Mac mini with a brand-new chip, the M6. And this time, it’s more focused on AI than ever. Unprecedented power in a tiny box. Impressive gaming for what it is. Big gains in some AI performance. Good port selection with support for dual 5K monitors.”
Gizmodo (4.5/5): “A Better Tiny Desktop, With or Without AI. The latest Mac mini offers unparalleled performance for its price. Just know the AI connoisseurs are waiting to gobble it up first.”
Petapixel (3.5/5): “The novelty of the M4-generation Mac mini’s redesign has worn off. But on the plus side, there’s something else all-new to enjoy, the first Mac with M6 is here.”
TechRadar hasn't reviewed the new Apple Mac mini yet.

articles.title: Hot Girl Hotline is like 'Dear Abby' for the AI era | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Women throughout history have always sought out relationship advice, whether from newspaper columnists like “Dear Abby,” letters to Cosmo, or just chatting with girlfriends. In the social media era, you can instead post anonymously on Reddit relationship forums or look to social media creators who discuss the topic.
Now, two sisters are launching a startup for young women, Hot Girl Hotline, which focuses on bringing AI into these conversations.
I know what you may be thinking: With all the advances in AI technology, founders are building something for women to talk about their dating woes? Well … yes!
The reality is that people have already been turning to large language models (LLMs) via apps like ChatGPT for this type of advice, and the team believes this type of activity should be handled more carefully.
Unfortunately, as we’ve seen, chatting with a general-purpose chatbot about personal topics can sometimes lead to disastrous effects — especially for those who were already mentally fragile. ChatGPT, for example, has faced a wave of lawsuits over its alleged manipulative conversation tactics that plaintiffs say contributed to negative mental health effects, including, in some cases, suicide.
The idea behind Hot Girl Hotline is to reach young women who are looking to have these sorts of private conversations while navigating dating life and relationships, but in a safer way.
“We’re not trying to be an AI companion,” explained Baila Mudgil, formerly a social media consultant, who co-founded the startup with her sister Sumrin (“Sumi”), who studied computer science at Stanford. “A companion is really going after solving loneliness, escapism, boredom — and you can rely on a lot of emotional dependency from that AI companion.”
Baila says the startup’s approach is to focus on offering quality advice grounded in behavioral science, but in a way that makes it feel like you’re chatting with a trusted friend or big sister. The conversation is often Socratic, with the AI asking you questions to help you arrive at the answer yourself.
“This is not to replace speaking to a human. This is not clinical advice, and we have a lot of safeguards in place … we take safety really seriously,” Baila said. If conversations raise flags, for instance, the user is referred to resources such as the crisis hotline 988.
“We believe the key to quality advice is not just knowing what to do next; it’s understanding why you’re doing it. So that’s a big piece of it,” added Sumi.
Notably, the AI also knows when to end the conversation; it doesn’t keep asking follow-up questions to drag you further down a rabbit hole. Instead, it pushes users to go take action out in the real world rather than ruminate on the problem.
The sisters believe there’s room for an app like this because not everyone wants to post on the web for advice, and there are times when you don’t want to bring up a personal, dating, or relationship-focused issue with a friend.
Friends can bring their own biases into the conversation, or the user may not want to put their partner on blast for something they did before they determine whether they’re going to work through it or end the relationship.
“It doesn’t mean you’re replacing your friend — you’re just trying to get another perspective,” says Baila of the hotline.
The app also personalizes its advice for each user to reflect their values, goals, identity, and tastes.
Under the hood, the startup relies on a mix of AI models and encrypts users’ data in transit and at rest. It doesn’t sell or train on the data, either. When it uses a third-party AI model, it follows a zero-data-retention policy there as well.
Hot Girl Hotline plans to monetize through a $9.99 per month subscription, which hundreds of its most active users are already paying for. Later, it may incorporate ads, too.
Relationship advice is just the beginning of how the company wants to cater to young women. It also plans to expand into other areas, like beauty and lifestyle.
New York-based Hot Girl Hotline is currently bootstrapped and will be participating in the Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco. It’s available on iOS and the web.

articles.title: Games-Nostalgie: Erstickt der Retro-Fokus die Spielebranche?
articles.text:
Witcher 3, Skyrim, Grand Theft Auto V: Warum Remakes so beliebt sind – und die Games-Industrie gefährden
Reboots von Filmfranchises, Fortsetzungen von Serienklassikern, Neuauflagen ikonischer Videospiele. Der Gedanke, wenn auch nur kurz, in eine einfachere, vermeintlich bessere Zeit zurückzuspringen, ist für viele Menschen reizvoll. Auch für mich. Wenn ich an meine liebsten Spiele überhaupt zurückdenke, steht ein Name ganz oben auf der Liste: Gothic. Ein episches Rollenspiel aus Deutschland, das meine Jugend um die Jahrtausendwende geprägt hat. Logisch, dass ich also trotz Erwachsenenverpflichtungen wie Arbeit dutzende Stunden in das vor wenigen Wochen erschienene Remake versenkt habe.
Die Neuauflage von Gothic ist nur ein Beispiel für die Remake-Wut, die auch die Spielebranche im Griff hat. Ob Neuinterpretationen von Quasi-Oldies wie Final Fantasy VII oder Titel wie Skyrim oder Grand Theft Auto V, die mit jeder neuen Konsolengeneration mindestens eine weitere Frischzellenkur spendiert bekommen: Altbewährtes scheint zu funktionieren. Auch die Ende September erschienene Neuauflage von The Witcher 3 fährt erwartbar Top–Wertungen ein. Das zeigt, wie gerne wir zurück statt nach vorn schauen. Denn letzteres könnte eher für mulmige Gefühle sorgen.
Seit der Corona-Pandemie haben unterschiedlicher Quellen zufolge jährlich zwischen 5.000 und 15.000 Spielearbeiter:innen ihre Jobs verloren. Alleine in seiner Xbox-Sparte hat Microsoft ganze Studios wegrationalisiert und über 3.000 Stellen gestrichen. Experimentiert wird in großen Spielefirmen immer seltener, Nintendo vielleicht mal außen vor. Das lässt sich natürlich nicht alleine mit der Nostalgieversessenheit der Spieler:innenschaft erklären. Wenn alles teurer wird, lassen sich 70 bis 90 Euro für ein Spiel eben schlechter rechtfertigen. Vor allem, wenn man nicht weiß, was man bekommt. Da greift man vielleicht eher zu etwas, was man schon kennt, statt etwas Neues zu probieren. Wie der Rückzug ins Altbekannte Wohlbefinden und soziale Verbundenheit verstärken kann, hat ein Team von Psychologen schon 2018 genauer unter die Lupe genommen.
Nostalgie in Videospielen: Zerstört der Retro-Boom der Games-Branche Innovation?
Der Blick zurück schlägt sich auch an anderer Stelle nieder. Denn statt sich mit neuen, frischen Spielideen zu beschäftigen, interessieren sich Spieler:innen mutmaßlich hauptsächlich für Fortsetzungen. Daten des Lobbyverbands Game für 2025 zufolge finden sich unter den Top 10 der meistverkauften Games in Deutschland neun direkte Sequels oder neue Titel aus alten Franchises. Auf Platz 13: das Remaster von Oblivion, dem Vorgänger von Skyrim.
Hinter all den Verkaufserfolgen stecken meistens große Konzerne wie Electronic Arts, Ubisoft oder Microsoft mit seinen Unterstudios Activision und Bethesda. Die haben jede Menge Marketingbudget, um ihre Sequel- und Reboot-Strategie in jeden noch so entfernten Winkel der Welt zu tragen. Und wie mächtig Nostalgie als Marketinginstrument sein kann, haben beispielsweise 2025 Wissenschaftler:innen der Uni Newcastle untersucht. Konzerne spielen also bewusst mit unserer Sehnsucht nach einer Welt, die mutmaßlich leichter zu begreifen war, und den Erlebnissen, die wir damit verbinden. Bei dem einen ist es ein Filmfranchise, bei der anderen eine Buchreihe, bei mir zum Beispiel Gothic.
Aber die Games-Industrie hat mehr zu bieten. Produktionen mit Millionenbudgets und der Hype um Grand Theft Auto VI, das von Netzkommentator:innen wahlweise als größtes Gaming-Event des Jahrhunderts oder kulturelles Mega-Phänomen bezeichnet wird, sind nämlich nur das eine. Meinen Appetit auf mehr Gothic konnte ich zum Beispiel im vergangenen Jahr mit dem deutschen Indie-Rollenspiel Drova stillen. Das sieht mit seinem Pixel-Look gänzlich anders aus, transportiert aber eine ähnliche Atmosphäre wie das Ruhrpott-Rollenspiel von 2001. Und es zeigt anekdotisch, dass beides geht: die guten, alten Zeiten aufzuwärmen und trotzdem offen zu sein für Neues. Wenn sich mehr Gamer:innen abseits der Charts umschauen und vielleicht endlich mal die lästige Fixierung auf Fotorealismus ablegen würden, könnte die Games-Branche auch wieder die Kurve kriegen – und trotzdem noch Platz für Nostalgie bieten.

articles.title: The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
articles.text:
The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it’s also now the first to escape the FCC’s Roomba ban.
The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
Unlike the router companies, Matic is publicly committing to US manufacturing.
Well, sort of — because the Matic wasn’t banned to begin with.
Here’s what’s actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and its charging dock model 4DK0008 to its ban waiver list. That allows the FCC to approve these radio products for import, marketing, and sale.
But the Matic doesn’t need a waiver, because its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC’s foreign drone, robot, and router bans only keep future products from getting imported into the United States, not existing ones whose radios have already been approved.
Besides, Matic’s products don’t get FCC approval to begin with — instead, Matic ships them with an off-the-shelf Intel AX210 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip that gets its own approval from the FCC. (It’s the same kind of Wi-Fi card you’ll find inside a desktop or laptop computer.) Matic also doesn’t need to worry about an import ban specifically, because Matic assembles its robots right here in Mountain View, California.
A waiver could theoretically help if Matic were to build new products outside the United States and try to import them here, except that the FCC hasn’t granted Matic a blanket approval on a brand of robot, like it did with Asus and Netgear’s routers. Instead, it specifically granted a waiver for the Matic models 4MA0001 and 4DK0008, which, again, have already made it through the FCC.
The waiver might not be completely symbolic. The FCC is currently trying to close lots of the loopholes that currently make its ban impotent, is weighing whether to make manufacturers disclose all the components in their gadgets, and is retroactively cracking down on some companies it sees as flaunting the rules. While Matic assembles its robots in the US, it admits it doesn’t yet source 65 percent of its components from US suppliers, the threshold for it to be seen as Made in the US, and perhaps one of those foreign components could trip it up if not for the waiver.
Even so, Matic already gets its “core compute platform” from Nvidia, co-founder and president Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge, and sources other “critical components” from US companies “whenever possible.”
And unlike some of the other companies where the FCC has mysteriously granted a waiver, Matic is committing to more US manufacturing and onshoring.
“Up till 3 months ago, both our R&D offices and production facilities were in the same office in Mountain View, about 24,000 square feet,” Nariyawala tells The Verge. “We’ve turned that entire facility into production facility and moved our office to Menlo Park.”
He says Matic went from shipping 1,500 robots a year ago to 17,000 now, and is trying to find more and more US suppliers so it can use even fewer foreign parts.
“At the moment we might be the only floor cleaning robot built in America,” he says. “That is becoming one of the key value propositions for our product.”
Correction: Nariyawala is Matic’s co-founder and president, not CEO.

articles.title: This is the worst laptop deal I’ve ever seen –why no one should by a laptop with 4GB of RAM in 2026
articles.text:
This laptop deal is selling fast at Argos — but whatever you do, DON’T buy it
No one should buy a 4GB RAM laptop in 2026
As we approach the end of the year, big sales events will begin cropping up regularly, culminating in Black Friday in November. This week, it's the Amazon Big Deals Days event, and I've just found what might just be the worst laptop deal of the year.
That's right, the worst. So why am I writing about it? Well, I think it's worth pointing out 'deals' that are actually a waste of money, and explain what makes those deals bad, to help you avoid getting stung in the future. Of course, I've also added some alternative laptop deals that are much better, and worth buying instead.
• Browse the full Amazon Prime Day sale
The awful laptop deal in question is for the HP 14-em0018na (what a great name for a product), that Argos is selling for £279.
Now, with prices for many devices climbing ever upwards, getting a Windows 11 laptop for under £300 might seem like fantastic value, but looking at the hardware involved, you should stay well clear.
The biggest red flag is that this laptop comes with just 4GB of RAM. That's a pitiful amount for a Windows 11 laptop in 2026 — these days I'd recommend 16GB as a minimum, with 8GB only being worth it if the laptop is really cheap.
Unlike ChromeOS, which Chromebooks run on, Windows 11 is a heavy (some might say 'bloated') operating system that needs a lot of memory to run smoothly, and 4GB just won't cut it. This laptop will be slow, unreliable and very annoying, especially if you want to run multiple apps at once.
The dual-core AMD Athlon 7120U processor is also pretty pathetic, and despite HP claiming the laptop has "plenty of storage", 128GB isn't going to last long these days, especially as most of that space will be taken up by Windows 11.
I'm annoyed at Argos selling this, as anyone buying it is likely going to feel ripped off. According to the Argos website, it seems this laptop is selling steadily as well, which is worrying. User reviews are positive, though vague (and one even admits they've not used it yet, but have still given it a high score), and I wonder if those impressions will be quite so positive after a few weeks of using the laptop.
Of course, budgets are tight at the moment, and not everyone can afford a high-end laptop packed with RAM and cutting-edge components, but there are plenty of cheap laptop deals out there that will offer much better value for money. So don't be tempted just because this laptop has a rock-bottom price tag — check out these laptop deals instead:
Today's best cheap laptop deals in the UK
Here's another HP laptop deal from Argos, and not only is it cheaper, it's just an all-round better buy. For a start, it's got twice the RAM, which will help make things feel quicker, and because it runs on Chrome OS, that extra RAM will make even more of a difference with how snappy it feels compared to a Windows 11 laptop with similar specs. If you're after the absolute lowest price possible, then a Chromebook like this is a great pick.
See? HP can make good cheap laptops, and Argos knows it. This laptop is just £20 more expensive but comes with double the RAM and storage (8GB and 256GB, respectively), and a more powerful Intel Core i3 processor. While it's still far from powerful, it'll be much better at handling day-to-day tasks, and should last a lot longer as well before you feel the need to upgrade.
This is another sub-£300 laptop that's worth considering. It's a Chromebook Plus device, which is more powerful than a regular Chromebook, so with a decent (for a Chromebook) 8GB of RAM and Intel Core 3 processor, you're going to have a much better experience than if it was a Windows 11 laptop with half the RAM. Just remember that Chrome OS doesn't support all the applications Windows 11 does, but there's often alternative software that is just as good.

articles.title: Connecting AI agents to enterprise knowledge
articles.text:
Sponsored
Connecting AI agents to enterprise knowledge
A strong structural foundation that links data and agents is key for context-rich agentic AI that scales.
In partnership withNeo4j
For all the data that AI systems continually amass and analyze, enterprise AI agents often suffer from a curious shortcoming: a lack of knowledge. More than data, knowledge is the understanding of what the data means in the context of individual organizations. AI agents need this understanding to reason about situations, make decisions, and ultimately take actions. Without sufficient knowledge, agents are prone to making flawed and unreliable decisions.
A lack of knowledge, our research finds, is a major reason agentic AI use cases never make it to production. Competitive pressure is making it urgent to address this. Organizations need to deploy and scale more of their agentic projects to capture the efficiency gains AI promises. Falling short risks wasting the investment already sunk into these projects, and it cedes ground to rivals already putting their agents to work more effectively.
The purpose of this report, which is based on a survey of 300 data, AI, and other technology executives, is threefold. First, it seeks to gauge organizations’ agentic knowledge capabilities (i.e., their ability to give AI agents a full contextual understanding of the data they ingest) across semantic knowledge, episodic memory, and procedural knowledge.
Second, the report probes the challenges organizations face in improving access to knowledge and ultimately to getting more agent use cases into production. Third, it explores the measures organizations are taking to overcome these challenges.
The key findings include the following:
Data and knowledge weaknesses consistently stall AI agent progress. On average, only around a third (34%) of organizations’ agentic AI projects make it into production. Even high-tech firms struggle with this. Legacy data systems, security and privacy concerns, and a lack of knowledge and context are the key points of failure.
Strong knowledge capabilities correlate with agent success. A small group of production leaders (organizations where on average 61% of agentic projects advance beyond pilot) have stronger knowledge capabilities than the rest, especially when it comes to semantics. This advantage tracks closely with their higher production rate.
Fragmented data hugely complicates knowledge access. Data fragmentation (the inadequate sharing of data across systems) was most commonly cited as a top challenge to expanding agents’ access to knowledge (cited by 55%). Production leaders, by contrast, are more likely to see security and privacy concerns as a major concern (cited by 72% of this group).
Most firms aim to strengthen the link between data and agents. Among steps that can yield higher quality agent decisions, executives expect the biggest impact to come from strengthening the structural foundation between the organization’s data and its AI agents. The experts we interviewed see a knowledge layer as a prime way to achieve this.
Investment priorities to boost knowledge range from pipelines to knowledge graphs. To expand agent access to knowledge, organizations will prioritize investments in retrieval technologies, like ingestion pipelines, AI-ready APIs, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); in AI evaluation agents; and in knowledge graphs.

articles.title: Neuer Computer zum Prime Day? Auf welche Komponenten es ankommt – und was du nicht brauchst
articles.text:
PC oder Laptop zu den Prime Deal Days kaufen? Auf welche Komponenten es ankommt – und was du nicht brauchst
Die Amazon Prime Deal Days bringen für Tech-Begeisterte, die sich nach neuem Equipment umschauen, zahlreiche Angebote mit sich. Doch gerade beim Kauf eines neuen Laptops oder PCs ist es schwierig, die Spreu vom Weizen zu trennen. Wer einfach nur „Laptop“ oder „PC“ in die Suchleiste bei Amazon eingibt, wird von einer Vielzahl von Produkten erschlagen.
Damit du in dem Chaos den Durchblick bewahren kannst, haben wir dir hier die wichtigsten Eckpunkte zum Kauf eines neuen Laptops oder PCs im Rahmen der Amazon Prime Days und darüber hinaus zusammengefasst. Dabei nehmen wir speziell die Mindestanforderungen in den Fokus. Was muss das Gerät haben, damit du es noch in den nächsten Jahren problemlos benutzen kannst? Je nach Einsatzgebiet benötigst du womöglich aber etwas mehr Leistung. Auch dazu findest du Hinweise in den jeweiligen Abschnitten.
Prime Day: Laptop oder PC?
Zunächst solltest du dir die Frage stellen, welches Gerät du eigentlich benötigst. Die Wahl des Formfaktors entscheidet schon eine Menge darüber, welche Komponenten du am Ende bekommst und wie leistungsfähig sie sind. Wenn du beispielsweise nach einem Laptop suchst, haben die Geräte natürlich den Vorteil, dass du sie überall mit hinnehmen kannst. Der Nachteil ist allerdings, dass Laptops oftmals etwas teurer als ihre Desktop-Pendants sind oder mit etwas schwächeren Komponenten auskommen müssen.
Desktop-PCs oder Macs sorgen hingegen anderweitig für Mehrkosten. Statt wie beim Laptop sämtliche Peripherie im Gerät integriert zu haben, musst du dich beim Desktop-PC noch darum kümmern. Heißt: Maus, Tastatur, ein Monitor, Lautsprecher oder ein Headset sowie eine Webcam müssen ebenfalls noch angeschafft werden, um ein komplettes Setup zu bekommen. Zudem verbrauchen Desktop-PCs in der Regel etwas mehr Energie. Dafür lassen sich PCs generell leichter aufrüsten und künftig mit neuen Komponenten versehen, statt sie komplett austauschen zu müssen.
Betriebssystem: macOS oder Windows?
Die zweite Frage dürfte für viele User:innen zum Prime Day schon geklärt sein, aber wir wollen sie dennoch nicht unerwähnt lassen. Schließlich ist es eine große Entscheidung, entweder in Apples Ökosystem zu investieren oder zu einem Windows-Gerät zu greifen. Bei Macs und Macbooks bist du im System von Apple verankert. Die Kompatibilität zu anderen Apple-Geräten ist hervorragend, aber etwa zu Android-Smartphones oder PCs mit anderem Betriebssystem etwas schwieriger. Dafür liefert Apple ein übersichtliches und leicht verständliches Betriebssystem, das zusätzlich durch seine Stabilität und Energieeffizienz glänzt.
Windows hingegen ist deutlich offener, bietet gerade bei etwas unbekannteren Anwendungen eine größere Auswahl und lässt mit etwas Tüftelei sogar alte Apps zu, die schon nicht mehr unterstützt werden. Zudem finden sich bei Windows-Laptops deutlich mehr Geräte auf dem Markt und damit auch verschiedenste Konfigurationen. Das macht die Auswahl nicht unbedingt leichter, aber gibt dir gerade bei einem festgesetzten Preisrahmen mehr Auswahl als bei Apple.
Prozessor: Power für den Alltag
Der Prozessor deines neuen PCs oder Laptops wird die meiste Arbeit im Alltag übernehmen. Wer auf eine alte CPU setzt, bekommt es mit einer unterwältigenden Performance, langen Wartezeiten und möglicherweise auch Stabilitätsproblemen bei einigen Anwendungen zu tun. Deshalb lohnt es sich, vorab genau hinzuschauen und sich zu informieren.
CPU-Auswahl bei Apple
Beim Prime Day fällt die Wahl für Apple-User:innen recht leicht. Denn Amazon bietet von offizieller Seite her nur Macbooks und Macs mit vergleichsweise neuen Prozessoren wie dem M5 oder M6 an. Beide haben ausreichend Power für Office-Aufgaben. Das Gleiche gilt für das Macbook Neo, das Einsteigermodell unter Apples Laptops. Der Budget-Laptop wurde speziell für Office-Aufgaben und das Surfen im Web konzipiert.
Ältere Prozessoren ab dem M4 werden nur über Dritte auf Amazon im gebrauchten Zustand angeboten. Ausnahme ist da noch der Mac Mini mit M4‑Chip. Dennoch ist der Preis des kompakten Macs fast identisch mit dem Nachfolger mit M5. Hier solltest du also die Finger vom älteren Modell lassen. Selbiges gilt im Übrigen auch für noch ältere Macbooks, die mit Intel-Chip verkauft werden. Sie sind nicht mehr zeitgemäß.
CPU-Auswahl bei Windows
Aufgrund der hohen Anzahl von Komponenten, die mit Windows kompatibel sind, ist die Antwort auf die CPU‑Frage nicht ganz so einfach wie bei Apple. Auch die Bezeichnungen geben nicht immer eins zu eins Aufschluss darüber, wie stark ein Prozessor ist. Ein Intel Core i3-12100F kann in vielen Bereichen ähnliche Leistungen erzielen, wie ein Core i9‑12900H.
Bevor wir dir also jede CPU empfehlen, die beim Prime Day noch relevant und leistungsstark sein könnte, empfehlen wir dir einfach ein Tool, um das Ganze selbst zu prüfen. Im CPU-Bereich der Webseite User Benchmark finden sich mehr als 1.400 getestete Prozessoren, deren Benchmarks von Nutzer:innen selbst ermittelt und hochgeladen wurden. Daraus ergibt sich ein Durchschnitt für die jeweilige CPU.
Zudem zeigt User Benchmark in den Bereichen Gaming, Office-Arbeit und Surfen, wie gut die jeweilige CPU wirklich ist. Du musst also nur den Namen der CPU in die Suchleiste eintragen und auf das Ergebnis klicken, um auf einen Blick zu sehen, ob der Prozessor deinen Ansprüchen genügt.
Arbeitsspeicher: Vorausschauend kaufen
Wer aktuell einen PC oder Laptop kauft, muss zwangsweise mit etwas höheren Preisen rechnen. Das liegt an der RAM-Krise, die laut Einschätzungen auch noch einige Jahre anhalten könnte. Die Nachfrage nach RAM-Riegeln übersteigt bei weitem das Angebot, wodurch die wenigen Produkte auf dem Markt teilweise einfach überteuert sind. Gerade die Prime Days könnten den Kauf durch Angebote wieder attraktiv machen.
Wichtig dabei ist, dass du keine Laptops und PCs kaufen solltest, die lediglich mit vier Gigabyte RAM ausgestattet sind. Davon gibt es noch einige, wenn auch wenige Modelle auf Amazon. Die Geräte sind zwar billig, dürften aber schlichtweg für die meisten Aufgaben nicht mehr up-to-date sein. Viele Office-Programme wie Word haben zwar vier Gigabyte RAM als Mindestanforderung, doch lassen sich die Geräte künftig oftmals nicht upgraden und mit mehr Speicher ausstatten, wenn du leistungsintensivere Apps für Bildbearbeitung und Videoschnitt nutzen möchtest.
Auch wenn du jetzt also etwas tiefer in die Tasche greifen musst, solltest du keinen Laptop oder PC kaufen, der weniger aösr acht Gigabyte RAM hat. 16 Gigabyte sind schon eher der Standard. Auch wenn sich die Geräte aufrüsten lassen, müsstest du sonst noch künftig in einen oder mehrere zusätzliche RAM‑Riegel investieren. Und da die Preise in absehbarer Zukunft nicht sinken und tendenziell eher steigen werden, wäre das unnötig herausgeworfenes Geld. 32 Gigabyte RAM sind allerdings auch eine zu hohe Investition, wenn du nicht gerade Aufgaben wie Videoschnitt regelmäßig nutzt oder anspruchsvolle Games in 4K-Auflösung mit den höchsten Grafikeinstellungen zocken willst.
Speicher: Schnell und ausreichend
Mittlerweile sollte eine SSD Pflicht sein, wenn du einen neuen PC oder Laptop kaufst. HDDs sollten nur noch als Massenspeicher für Daten infrage kommen. Sie als Bootmedium für die Installation von Windows zu nutzen, ist schlichtweg veraltet. Leider ist es bei Windows-PCs und ‑Laptops oftmals schwer ersichtlich, welche SSD im Gerät zum Einsatz kommt. Die Hersteller geben meist nur die Kapazität an. Das Problem: Gerade inoffizielle Anbieter, die zusammengebaute PCs anbieten, sparen beim Speicher und wählen ältere Modelle, die günstiger sind.
Deshalb solltest du unbedingt einen Blick in die Produktbeschreibung werfen. Wird dort kein Hersteller für den Speicher angegeben, hilft noch ein Blick in die Bewertungen. Beschweren sich andere User:innen über langsame Datentransfers oder lange Windows-Ladezeiten, solltest du nach einem anderen Produkt schauen. Etwas leichter haben es da alle Apple-Fans. Da der Speicher bis auf die Kapazität weitestgehend einheitlich ist, musst du dich lediglich entscheiden, wie viel Speicherplatz du benötigst.
Als Standard gilt – egal, ob Macs oder Windows-Geräte – mittlerweile ein Terabyte Speicher. Das reicht für die meisten Anwendungen und zum Speichern einer Vielzahl von Bildern, Dokumenten und Co. Willst du auch hochauflösende Videodateien speichern oder aufwendigere Games zocken, sollten es schon mindestens zwei Terabyte sein.
Konnektivität: Die richtigen Anschlüsse
Moderne PCs und Laptops sollten nicht mehr ausschließlich auf USB 2.0 setzen. Stattdessen sind USB-3-0-Anschlüsse mittlerweile Standard. Über sie können deutlich schneller Daten transferiert werden. Zudem solltest du darauf achten, dass PCs oder Laptops, die du an externe Monitore anschließen willst, mindestens einen HDMI-Anschluss haben. Alternativ können sie auch über Thunderbolt 4 angeschlossen werden, falls der Monitor den moderneren Anschluss unterstützt.
Für den heimischen Betrieb am Schreibtisch ist zudem ein Ethernetanschluss (LAN-Anschluss) empfehlenswert. Bist du mit deinem Laptop vornehmlich im WLAN unterwegs, ist er aber nicht zwingend notwendig und kann über USB-Dongles nachgerüstet werden. Bei WLAN-Verbindung solltest du darauf achten, dass das Gerät am besten schon Wi-Fi 6 unterstützt. Der WLAN-Standard setzt sich immer mehr durch. Dein PC oder Laptop bleibt so länger mit neueren Routern und anderen Geräten kompatibel.

articles.title: Cyber resilience now depends on governing AI agent data use - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Storage admins get automated guardrails as agents outrun human-in-the-loop review
Enterprises pushing AI agents into production are finding that cyber resilience now depends as much on governing what autonomous software does with data as on keeping attackers out. Much of the risk doesn’t come from malicious intent at all; it comes from agents doing unexpected things at machine speed.
That shift is pushing storage providers to build intelligent data infrastructure that can judge how data is being used. NetApp Inc. is moving access controls away from simple yes-or-no permissions and toward policies based on behavior, according to Russell Fishman (pictured), senior director of global AI solutions and field activation of NetApp.
“We’re starting to get away from thinking about everything through a human lens,” Fishman said. “This is an agent. Agents don’t think the same way. They’re not acting the same way.”
Fishman spoke with theCUBE’s Christophe Bertrand and Rebecca Knight at NetApp INSIGHT, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed a week of NetApp announcements, including Novus, a new storage architecture for AI factories and neoclouds, and the growing importance of cyber resilience as the market matures. (* Disclosure below.)
Cyber resilience moves into the data layer
NetApp’s traditional protection tools still carry weight as threats speed up. Its autonomous ransomware protection service uses AI to detect and block attacks, and a newly announced integration feeds those signals into recovery workflows from Commvault Systems Inc., Fishman explained. NetApp has built similar links with Microsoft Corp.’s Sentinel and Cisco Systems Inc.’s Splunk, he added.
“We become an indicator of compromise,” he said. “We can actually detect things and tell Commvault, ‘hey, there’s a problem,’ and vice versa.”
AI agents raise a different problem. Most organizations Fishman talks with worry less about bad actors than about agents causing unintended consequences while they try to finish an assigned task. New features in NetApp’s AI Data Engine, which prepares and governs enterprise data for AI, include a behavior-based policy engine that flags unusual patterns of data use, he noted.
“I would expect you to look at maybe one customer’s account, not all of the customers’ accounts,” he said. “That seems a bit weird to me.”
Responding at the speed of AI means organizations can’t always keep a human in the loop, so automation has to carry more of the load, Fishman explained. For NetApp customers who want stronger cyber resilience now, AI Data Engine can be deployed against any existing NetApp system, and the company announced a free six-month offer at the event, according to Fishman.
“If I was an ONTAP admin — if I was a NetApp customer — that’s the first thing I’d be doing,” Fishman said. “I want to lock this down now. The risk of not doing so, not just from a lack of innovation, but the risk of misuse of data, the lack of control, it’s too great.”

articles.title: Advancing The CFET-Based Device Roadmap: Novel Integration Modules And Standard Cell Configurations
articles.text:
Part 2: Towards scalable sCFET standard cell architectures: split-gate devices, a 5T+1 CFET SRAM bit cell, and improved back-end-of-line routability.
Key takeaways:
The semiconductor industry is going through a major architectural transition, with gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors replacing FinFETs in advanced logic nodes of 3nm and beyond. GAA nanosheet transistor technology offers scalability down to the A10 logic generation, where it enables 5.5-track (T) standard cells – the track being a measure for the standard cell height.
For the A7 node, options are becoming increasingly diverse to meet the growing diversification of application needs, driven by the AI revolution. According to imec’s latest roadmap, one option is to design systems around imec’s CMOS 2.0 scaling paradigm. With CMOS 2.0, a system-on-chip (SoC) is partitioned into heterogeneous, functional tiers each optimized using the most suitable technology, and reconnected using 3D interconnect technologies. For other use cases, GAA nanosheet technology may be pushed to its ultimate scaling limits, with power delivered from either the frontside or the backside. But industry may as well transition to complementary FET (CFET) device architectures. By stacking p and nMOS transistors on top of each other, standard cells can be further scaled down to 3T, thereby extending the classical CMOS logic roadmap to at least the A3 technology node.
Fig. 1: Imec’s logic technology roadmap.
Imec and its industrial partners are working to make CFET-based devices manufacturable. In recent years, they laid the groundwork for key integration approaches, categorized as monolithic CFET (mCFET) and sequential CFET (sCFET) [1,2].
Both approaches start from the vertical stacking of Si/SiGe layers from which the n and pFETs are fabricated. With mCFET, the vertical device structure with common top and bottom gates is patterned and processed in a single sequence of process steps. The patterning, deposition and selective removal of materials around and in between the high-aspect ratio device structure requires considerable effort in terms of module development. sCFET, on the contrary, patterns the top and bottom devices independently using dedicated masks. With sCFET, the individual process steps are simpler compared to mCFET but some critical steps need to be executed twice – for top and bottom separately. sCFET additionally involves two wafer flips, distorting the wafer and challenging the precise alignment of front-to-back device connections. Pending further progress in alignment accuracy, mCFET is believed to offer the fastest path to industrial adoption.
Progress in CFET integration is complemented with design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) studies that examine CFET device architectures from a circuit level perspective [2]. These studies aim to identify scalable standard cell configurations and performance boosters that offer the best tradeoff in terms of power, performance, area and cost.
In this 2-part article, we report major progress in CFET device integration, and we discuss CFET scalability using DTCO studies.
In part 1 [link], two process modules were presented that are essential for both mCFET and sCFET device flavors: (1) a backside contact module, and (2) a gate stack integration approach that enables multiple threshold voltages (Vt) in nanosheet and CFET devices.
In part 2, a scalable architecture for sCFET is introduced, allowing both split-gate and common-gate configurations. Besides progressing the logic roadmap, DTCO work shows how this split-gate architecture also benefits CFET-based SRAM scaling. Finally, improved back-end-of-line (BEOL) routability is demonstrated, supporting the scaling of CFET standard cells.
The reported results are achieved in the framework of the imec-hosted European NanoIC pilot line, which is targeting the development of beyond-2nm systems-on-chip. CFET development, which is centered on CFET-specific designs, process steps, modules and baseline flows, has been selected as one of the key enabling technologies for extending the logic roadmap into the ångström era. This will help Europe to remain at the forefront of next-generation semiconductor innovation and manufacturing.
Earlier DTCO studies have already demonstrated the scaling potential of CFET technology across subsequent logic nodes – a prerequisite for the semiconductor industry to adopt the new device architecture. For mCFET, for example, imec previously identified the double-row (DR) CFET architecture as the most optimal way to integrate mCFETs into an A7 standard cell [3]. A double-row CFET standard cell contains two rows of stacked devices with a shared vertical signal via in between, and power walls at the cell boundary (see Figure 2). Later, layout inefficiencies were addressed, resulting in an optimized version of the double-row CFET: the half-height double-row (hDR) architecture. At IEDM 2025, additional scaling boosters such as the integration of hybrid channels were introduced to support aggressive area scaling targets towards A3 [2].
The process flow for fabricating mCFET devices inherently offers common-gate devices: the gates of n and pFETs are structurally connected to one another. This works well for 90-95% of all basic logic gates – think about an inverter circuit (or NOT gate) that performs the logical operation of negation. But for other logic circuits, such as flipflops and multiplex gates, independent control of n and pFET metal gates is desired. One way to address this need is to leave one polarity of the stacked CFET device unused (for example, only using the nFETs, and removing the pFETs). While this approach solves the gate control issue, it does not fully exploit the area benefit of stacking n and pFETs.
sCFET device architectures, where top and bottom devices are patterned independently, can offer split-gate devices in a more natural way. But conventional sCFET architectures leave us with the opposite problem: an extra module is needed to connect the gates for those circuits that need it.
At 2026 VLSI, imec introduces the double-flip sCFET architecture that offers both split-gate and common-gate device options without compromising area efficiency [4].
Fig. 2: Cross-sectional views of (a) double-row mCFET (DR), (b) half-height double-row (hDR) with dense backside metal-0 tracks (BM0), (c) hDR with split gate, and (d) sCFET with split-gate and dense BM0 (as presented at 2026 VLSI). (CH = standard cell height; NSH = nanosheet channels; MRW = shared signal wall; VMM = via that can bypass the bottom device; MD = metal-to-diffusion layer)
The impact of the new architecture in terms of area efficiency and routability was evaluated for various CFET-based libraries, designed around, for example, AND, OR and inverter circuits. With an overall library efficiency (h) as high as 98%, the new sCFET double-flip architecture provides the most efficient area utilization compared to double-row (DR) and half-height double-row (hDR) mCFET architectures. When combined with dense backside metal-0 (BM0) routing, the new architecture supports 3T standard cells that will be needed in A3 and A2 logic nodes – according to imec’s latest technology roadmap.
Fig. 3: Cell area breakdown of CFET libraries, for each of the CFET architectures (double row (DR), half-height double-row (hDR), hDR with dense backside metal-0 routing (hDR/dense BMO), and double-flip sCFET). sCFET significantly optimizes cell library and achieves an overall 98% layout efficiency (hlayout) (as presented at 2026 VLSI).
The double-flip sCFET flow starts from a bonded stack with an embedded middle dielectric isolation (eMDI) between top and bottom devices [2]. First, the top device is patterned from the frontside, and the top gate is finished partly during the replacement metal-gate module. After wafer flip and wafer thinning, the bottom device is patterned from the backside. Next, a via connection between bottom and top gate is optionally provided, which can be utilized for common-gate use cases. Following a second wafer flip, processing of the top and bottom devices is completed.
Additional scaling potential is offered by the possibility to introduce hybrid channels, optimized for n and pFETs separately. Think about CFET devices with different channel orientations for the top and bottom devices, or CFETs with asymmetric sheet widths. This brings along extra power-performance-area benefits and supports design flexibility.
Static random-access memory (SRAM) continues to be industry’s main workhorse for providing on-chip cache memory – the high-speed memory that interfaces between dynamic RAM (DRAM) and XPU. A conventional SRAM memory bit cell consists of six transistors: four nFETs and two pFETs (or, alternatively, two nFETs and four pFETs). Of these FETs, two nFETs and two pFETs (PUx and PDx in Figures 5 and 6) are paired to form two cross-coupled inverters, able to store one bit of information. The remaining nFETs are designed as pass-gate transistors (PGs), connecting to the bit and word lines (BL, WL) and controlling the data flow during the read and write operations.
Just as in logic technology, the density increase of SRAM memory relies on dimensional scaling of the bit cells, in combination with device architecture innovations. But since the 7nm technology node, SRAM bit cell scaling has fallen flat compared to logic CMOS device scaling. This asymmetry in scaling potential presents considerable challenges for chip designers. Even the transition to GAA-nanosheet-based 6T SRAM cells could not provide the required power, performance, and area benefits. CFET-based 6T SRAM technology is expected to bring initial relief, as the stacking of (part of) the n and pFETs (i.e., PUx and PDx) can substantially increase the SRAM bit cell density.
Fig. 4: The SRAM density crisis. The blue symbols represent imec’s options for high-density SRAMs, including single row, double-row, optimized double-row, and the new 5T+1 architecture (as presented at 2026 VLSI).
But even in the CFET SRAM era, further area reduction is being challenged, as the 6T SRAM bit cell does not map efficiently onto a CFET-based architecture. While the two inverters can be mapped using a stacked n/p device architecture (PUx and PDx), the two nFETs serving as the single pass-gate transistors (PGs) leave the two top p-type transistors of the CFET device stack unused. As a result, the intrinsic vertical density advantage of CFET cannot fully translate into bit cell area scaling for a 6T SRAM. A 5T SRAM bit cell configuration with only one single pass-gate transistor has been investigated as an area-efficient alternative, but writability and noise issues have challenged its adoption.
Fig. 5: Schematic representation of a conventional 6T SRAM, which does not map nicely onto a CFET (as presented at 2026 VLSI). (WL = word lines; BL and BLB = bit lines; PUx and PDx form the cross-coupled invertors storing 1 bit of information; VSS and VDD are power supply lines)
Imec’s novel sCFET architecture for split-gate devices now opens doors to continued SRAM density scaling – as presented at 2026 VLSI [5]. In a novel 5T+1 architecture, the two single pass-gate transistors (PGs) are replaced with one CFET transmission-gate device (TG) that pairs an nFET and a pFET. Such a transmission gate needs independent n and p gate control, which can be enabled by implementing imec’s novel sCFET split-gate device. As such, a 5T-like SRAM bit cell (i.e., a single-ended SRAM bit cell with sCFET transmission gate) can be realized while maintaining a 5T footprint. The use of the transmission gate as the access device also improves writability compared to a ‘classic’ 5T implementation.
Fig. 6: Schematic representation of a 5T+1 CFET SRAM with transmission gate (as presented at 2026 VLSI). (BL = bit line; WLn and WLp are word lines connecting to the n and p FETs of the transmission gate (TG); VSS and VDD are power supply lines)
SRAM operation can be further improved by optimizing layout and routability at the memory array level. By using this innovative 5T+1 configuration, imec’s DTCO study shows a 12.5% smaller bit cell compared to a conventional 6T CFET SRAM cell, with 7-15% faster write operation. This makes the 5T+1 CFET SRAM bit cell an attractive option for prolonging the SRAM scaling roadmap towards A7 and beyond.
In various DTCO studies, imec has demonstrated the ability to scale CFET device architectures across subsequent logic technology nodes, supported by innovative standard cell configurations and scaling boosters. But as we approach the ångström era, the area advantages at standard cell level can easily be undone by scaling issues in the BEOL, following a new DTCO study presented by imec at 2026 VLSI [6]. In other words: it becomes increasingly difficult to interconnect the various CFET-based standard cells.
Under the ideal scaling scenario where everything scales proportionally, routability stays the same from one node to another. However, starting from the 2nm node, the scaling of some of the ground rules such as the contact poly pitch (CPP, a metric determined by both the gate length and source/drain contact length) and metal-1 pitch has started to slow down. And this increases routing congestion in the wafer frontside, which affects performance, power and area. In addition, aggressive standard cell scaling limits accessibility to the input and output pins.
Fortunately, there are several knobs for improving the BEOL routability. One of these is enhancing the so-called gear ratio, which represents the ratio of the CPP to the metal-1 pitch. In 2nm node processor designs, this gear ratio is usually around 1:1. At 2026 VLSI, imec demonstrated through a DTCO study that increasing the gear ratio to 2:1 for A7 CFET-based designs can improve both pin accessibility and area utilization, without compromising power and performance [6]. In practice, this will drive the metal 1 to smaller pitches, requiring more advanced lithography options like single-patterning High NA EUV lithography for its fabrication.
Fig. 7: Schematic representation of M1 routing for ND2D1 cells in A7 with GR 1:1 and GR 2:1, showing improved pin accessibility for GR 2:1 (as presented at 2026 VLSI).
With the double-flip sCFET, imec is introducing a new CFET device architecture into the logic roadmap. Double-flip sCFET has a high scaling potential, offering both split-gate and common-gate device options without area penalty. The novel architecture not only benefits the logic roadmap, but it also provides a solution for the stalled SRAM roadmap by enabling a 5T+1 SRAM CFET bit cell memory. In another DTCO study, imec shows how improved BEOL routability can further support the aggressive scaling of CFET based standard cells.
This work has been enabled in part by the NanoIC pilot line. For more information, visit nanoic-project.eu.

[2] ‘Performance boosters to scale monolithic CFET across multiple logic technology nodes,’ S. Yang et al., imec Reading Room, 2025;
[3] ‘Imec proposes double-row CFET for the A7 technology node,’ imec Press Release, 2024;
[4] ‘Double-flip sequential CFET: superior 3T library efficiency and PPA,’ S. Yang et al., 2026 VLSI;
[5] ‘5T+1 CFET SRAM with dual-bitline-per-cell-height enabling differential readout and 12.5% area reduction,’ D. Abdi, 2026 VLSI;
[6] ‘Scaling high density designs towards Angstrom nodes: BEOL routability, pin accessibility challenges and impact of gear ratio,’ J.-Y. Lin, 2026 VLSI.

articles.title: Gemin va connaitre un changement majeur le 9 octobre (et ce n'est pas une bonne nouvelle)
articles.text:
Google annonce qu’il va revoir la grille des modèles de Gemini et modifie les limites d’utilisation en fonction des abonnements. Ces ajustements, qui arrivent ce 9 octobre, touchent aussi bien les comptes gratuits que les comptes payants à Google AI. Le système de calcul repose désormais sur de nouveaux quotas toutes les cinq heures en fonction de la complexité des requêtes, de la longueur des échanges et des fonctionnalités activées.
Google revoit à la baisse certains modèles Gemini en fonction de votre abonnement
L’organisation des modèles de Gemini disponibles change pour chaque type de compte. Les personnes qui utilisent l’application gratuitement se voient désormais limitées au modèle Flash-Lite. Du côté des abonnés payants, la formule AI Plus donne accès uniquement au modèle Flash, perdant ainsi l’accès aux modèles Pro. Seuls les utilisateurs qui ont les abonnements AI Pro et AI Ultra conservent l’accès aux modèles Pro.
Chaque modèle disponible permet de régler un niveau d’effort (bas, moyen ou haut) afin d’obtenir des réponses plus poussées, ce qui consomme tout de même une part plus importante du quota global. Les abonnés aux formules AI Pro et AI Ultra profitent en prime de l’option « Deep Think » pour un raisonnement plus avancé.
Des nouveaux quotas de calcul
Le mode de calcul des limites d’utilisation prend désormais en compte la complexité des requêtes, la longueur des conversations et les outils mobilisés. Les fonctionnalités avancées exigent davantage de ressources et épuisent le quota plus rapidement, comme la génération de médias (images, vidéos et musique), de la recherche avancée, de l’utilisation du modèle Pro ou de la réflexion prolongée et du Deep Think.
À lire : Gemini 4 Argon s’attaque à ChatGPT et Claude : Google dévoile son IA la plus puissante
Les volumes autorisés dépendent, là encore, de la formule souscrite. Sans plan payant, les limites standard s’appliquent. L’abonnement AI Plus double ces seuils avec des limites deux fois plus élevées et la formule AI Pro les multiplie par quatre. Enfin, le niveau AI Ultra propose des quotas entre cinq et vingt fois ceux de la formule Pro, selon le niveau du mode Ultra auquel vous êtes abonné.

articles.title: 5 startups that caught VCs' attention at the latest PearX demo day | TechCrunch
articles.text:
There isn’t a shortage of accelerators for startups, but one of the few that investors watch closely is PearX, a 12-week program that caps its cohorts at a mere 20 startups and is run by Pear VC, a pre-seed and seed-focused venture firm.
PearX’s biannual demo day is consistently attended by top venture capitalists, reflecting the historically strong caliber of companies in each batch. Some of the startups that came out of recent cohorts include Known, which uses voice AI to match people for dates and secured funding from Forerunner Ventures. Another is Andera, a startup that automates corporate audit and compliance tasks and raised a $37 million Series A from Lightspeed this summer.
The PearX program distinguishes itself from Y Combinator, the OG of startup accelerators, in several ways. Besides being much smaller, it doesn’t offer companies standard terms. Its investments can be as high as $2 million. Moreover, unlike YC, where some of the buzziest startups raise funding before the program ends, PearX claims to keep its participants under wraps until demo day.
TechCrunch attended Pear’s latest demo day, which took place in San Francisco last week, and then stuck around to ask some of the VCs about which companies stood out to them out of the 16 startups in the batch.
Below are five of the companies that seemed to have generated the most buzz.
Speridlabs
What it does: Spatial foundational models for powering robotics, gaming, and special effects.
Why it stood out: While Speridlabs is certainly not the only startup developing world models to do for 3D space what LLMs did for language, it argues that its more established competitors, including Runway, Odyssey, and Google’s Genie, cannot be queried or modified. To solve this, Speridlabs built Mundus, which it calls a 3D Midjourney because it keeps its geometry persistent when a part is changed.
Saia
What it does: Builds a fast, cost-efficient chip that runs inference directly on device.
Why it stood out: Nvidia’s GPUs and Google’s TPUs require expensive, power-hungry memory that is currently in short supply. Saia claims to have designed a chip that bypasses traditional memory by running AI directly out of flash storage. The startup claims its chip delivers vastly superior speeds and eight times the capacity while using four times less power than Nvidia’s Jetson, a leading local AI chip and board. Saia says it’s already in discussions with Samsung regarding memory integration, plans to start fabricating test chips next year, and aims to launch mass production by 2028. Developing hardware is notoriously brutal, but 20-year-old founder Ayaan Govil managed to convince Pear VC co-founder Mar Hershenson, a semiconductor engineer with a PhD in circuit design, to take a chance on his vision.
Ren
What it does: A more secure AI personal assistant.
Why it stood out: Ren claims to offer functionality similar to Muse and Instinct, but with a heavy focus on security and privacy. The startup says it keeps data on-device where possible or uses a secure private cloud, checking actions against strict user-set guardrails. Furthermore, Ren distinguishes itself from competitors that rely on human operators to place phone calls by using a fully automated voice system, keeping human involvement entirely out of the loop to protect user privacy.
Veros
What it does: AI native trust and estate planner.
Why it stood out: Setting up a trust is expensive and time-consuming. Veros wants to simplify the work normally done by attorneys, wealth managers, and trust administrators by employing AI to recommend structures and manage assets over their lifetime. Already managing $250 million in AUM, the startup is also in the process of securing a trust charter so it can operate as a regulated trust company itself.
Datum
What it does: AI engineer for industrial design.
Why it stood out: Datum wants to expedite physical product development by helping engineers find and use what they built previously. The startup indexes a company’s library of 3D designs. Using proprietary Geometric Fingerprint technology, Datum identifies parts based on their shape, helping streamline and automate engineering across a massive physical design market.

articles.title: Amazon lance les Jours Flash Prime et ça commence ce soir !
articles.text:
Amazon lance demain, mardi 6 octobre à 0h01, ses Jours Flash Prime. Pendant 48 heures, les membres Prime auront accès à des centaines de milliers d'offres, à quelques semaines du Black Friday. Voici ce qu'il faut savoir avant le coup d'envoi.
Une nouvelle édition des Jours Flash Prime avant le Black Friday
L'événement commence le mardi 6 octobre à 00h01 et se termine le mercredi 7 octobre à 23h59. Les promotions durent donc 48 heures et pas une minute de plus ! Cette édition d'automne suit le Prime Day de juin. À l'étranger, Amazon l'appelle Prime Big Deal Days. Amazon lance l'opération dans 22 pays, dont la France, l'Allemagne, l'Espagne, l'Italie, le Royaume-Uni, les États-Unis et le Japon.
Comment profiter des ventes flash Amazon ?
Les offres sont réservées aux membres Prime. L'abonnement coûte 6,99 € par mois ou 69,90 € par an, avec 30 jours d'essai gratuit pour les nouveaux membres. Un nouvel abonné peut donc s'inscrire avant le début de l'événement et profiter des offres pendant l'essai.
A quoi s'attendre côté bons plans pour ce Prime Day d'automne ?
Amazon annonce des centaines de milliers de promotions dans de nombreux rayons : décoration, arts de la table, mode, jeux et jouets, beauté, cuisine, électronique et produits du quotidien. Parmi les marques citées figurent Bosch, Bose, Groupe Seb, LG, Lego, Lunii, Ninja, Oral-B, Philips et Samsung.
Côté high-tech, on peut s'attendre à de fortes remises sur les appareils Amazon (Echo, Fire TV, Kindle, Ring, Blink, eero), dont une partie est en promotion depuis le 29 septembre. Des remises allant jusqu'à -70% sont évoquées, mais elles ne concernent pas tous les produits.
Certaines promos ont déjà commencé. Notre sélection de 30 offres tech couvre les liseuses, la maison connectée, les aspirateurs robots, le smartphone, la photo, l'audio et la recharge, avec des remises allant jusqu'à -60%. Un relevé précédent avait déjà noté des remises de -5% à -58%, calculées à partir des prix barrés affichés par Amazon.
Devenir membre Prime : des avantages toute l'année
Les Jours Flash Prime ne sont qu'une partie de l'abonnement. Pour 6,99 € par mois ou 69,90 € par an, Prime donne accès toute l'année à la livraison gratuite en 1 jour ouvré sur les articles éligibles, à Prime Video, à Amazon Music, à Prime Gaming et au stockage illimité de photos sur Amazon Photos. Voici ce que comprend l'abonnement :
- Livraison en 1 jour ouvré gratuite et illimitée sur des millions d'articles éligibles, en France métropolitaine (hors Corse) et en Belgique. Le site annonce aussi un service de Monaco, sans minimum de commande.
- Livraison le soir même à Paris, Lille, Lyon, Marseille, Rouen et Strasbourg, entre autres, pour les commandes éligibles de 35 € ou plus.
- Réductions « Prévoyez et Économisez » sur certains produits livrés régulièrement à la même adresse.
- Événements réservés aux membres, comme le Prime Day et les Jours Flash Prime.
- Accès prioritaire aux Ventes Flash, 30 minutes avant leur démarrage officiel pour les offres éligibles.
Livraison planifiée gratuite, jusqu'à 7 jours à l'avance.
Nos conseils pour bien préparer l'événement
- Vérifiez que votre abonnement Prime est actif, ou lancez l'essai gratuit de 30 jours avant minuit.
- Ajoutez vos produits à la liste d'envies pour retrouver vite les baisses de prix.
- Soyez réactif sur les produits les plus demandés, car les stocks partent vite.
- Pensez aux coupons. Il faut cocher la case affichée sous le prix, sur la fiche produit, avant d'ajouter l'article au panier. La réduction s'applique ensuite au paiement.
- Comparez avec l'historique des prix. Un prix barré n'indique pas toujours une vraie économie, et une remise très forte peut venir d'un prix de référence gonflé.
Les Jours Flash Prime en direct avec Clubic
Du 6 au 7 octobre, l'équipe Clubic Bons Plans suit l'événement en direct :
- Sélections par catégories et par marques
- Offres mises à jour en temps réel
- Produits testés ou recommandés par nos experts.
Pour ne rien rater, vous pouvez aussi suivre @ClubicBonsPlans sur X afin d’être alerté en direct des meilleures promos avant les ruptures de stock.

articles.title: Bringing predictive analytics to the agentic AI era
articles.text:
Sponsored
Bringing predictive analytics to the agentic AI era
Predictive modeling with AI can revolutionize how organizations use everyday business data.
In association withTP
In 2026, the question for enterprise AI is no longer whether predictive models can outperform statistical forecasts—that argument is settled. The big question now is how to enable predictive systems to act on their own conclusions without drifting from business intent. The frontier has moved from prediction to autonomous decision making, and the gap between leaders and laggards is widening accordingly.
“Enterprises are done with a backward-looking point of view; they want to be more forward-thinking,” says Vishal Gupta, partner at research firm Everest Group.
Intelligent analytics, powered by technologies like deep learning and generative AI, are making this possible. Real-time training allows AI to evolve continuously instead of waiting for quarterly refreshes. In addition, the data that newer predictive engines rely upon has expanded to encompass not just neat, numerical records but also messy, unstructured sources of insight-rich interactions. As a result, AI-powered analytics are moving enterprises from passive hindsight to pragmatic foresight.
AI takes predictive analytics—a broad discipline that includes predictive modeling, data prep, analysis workflows, interpretation of results, and decision-making applications—to new heights. “In many ways I think the word ‘analytics’ is giving way to AI,” says Gupta. “Everything is becoming AI.”
