articles.title: « Éviter les chatons gris sur le bitume gris » : pourquoi les robotaxis Tesla ne roulent pas toute la nuit
articles.text:
Dans la soirée du vendredi 2 octobre, le compte officiel du service Robotaxi de Tesla a annoncé qu’à Austin, au Texas, les taxis sans chauffeur de la marque ne prendront plus de courses après 23 heures, au lieu de 22 heures auparavant. Elon Musk a relayé l’annonce sur X et a expliqué ce qui empêche ses voitures de rouler plus tard.
Selon lui, Tesla cherche avant tout à « ne pas écraser d’animaux de compagnie quand ils sont difficiles à voir la nuit », autrement dit à éviter « littéralement des chatons gris sur du bitume gris dans le noir ». C’est la première fois que le patron de Tesla reconnaît publiquement que l’obscurité limite son service commercial.
Malgré cette heure en plus, Austin reste en dessous de ses horaires de départ. Au lancement, le 22 juin 2025, Tesla prenait des courses de 6h du matin à minuit, avec un employé assis à la place passager. Depuis fin août 2026, le service tourne de 6h à 22h dans les six villes où les voitures roulent sans employé à bord : Austin, Dallas et Houston au Texas, puis Miami, Orlando et Tampa en Floride. Mais sur toutes ces villes, Austin est la seule à passer à 23h.
Tesla a tout misé sur les caméras
Le problème décrit par Elon Musk est connu depuis longtemps, la caméra est un capteur passif. Elle enregistre la lumière renvoyée par un objet et le repère grâce au contraste avec ce qui l’entoure. La nuit, un chat gris sur une route grise lui renvoie très peu de lumière et presque aucun contraste, donc risque de ne pas être détecté par le système.
En réponse à un internaute qui a demandé si une caméra thermique ne serait pas utile, Elon Musk explique que « les caméras à spectre visuel voient très bien dans l’obscurité lorsque l’IA effectue l’analyse du comptage des photons ». En d’autres termes, le logiciel analyse ce qu’il voit en comptant les photons individuels (les particules de lumière) qui frappent chaque pixel de la caméra. Apparemment, l’analyse n’est encore assez poussée pour permettre le fonctionnement des robotaxis de Tesla 24h/24.
Pour analyser leur environnement, la plupart des autres véhicules autonomes ajoutent à leur caméra une flopée de radars et de LiDAR. Ce dernier utilise la technologie laser en envoyant des impulsions tout autour puis mesurant le temps qu’elles mettent à revenir. Il obtient ainsi une exacte représentation d’un objet et sa distance, aussi bien à minuit qu’à midi. Avec ce genre d’appareil, un chat gris dans la nuit ne serait plus vraiment un problème.
Cependant, croyant en l’efficacité absolue des caméras uniquement, Tesla a retiré le radar de ses voitures en mai 2021, puis les capteurs à ultrasons en 2022. Cette philosophie « Vision Only » se poursuit naturellement avec les taxis autonomes de la firme américaine. En avril 2019, Elon Musk assurait que « quiconque s’appuie sur le lidar est condamné ». En mai dernier encore, il se vantait que le FSD, le logiciel de conduite autonome supervisée de Tesla, voie « si bien la nuit ».
De son côté, le concurrent le plus sérieux, Waymo, fait rouler ses robotaxis en combinant trois technologies (caméras, LiDAR et radars) et ce, jusqu’au bout de la nuit sans interruption. Sa sixième génération de capteurs, présentée en août 2024, compte 13 caméras, 4 LiDAR et 6 radars.
Le 4 septembre, Ashok Elluswamy, qui dirige le logiciel d’IA de Tesla, avait promis un service 24 heures sur 24 pour le mois prochain ou à peu près, grâce à la version 15 du FSD. Un mois plus tard, une seule ville a gagné une heure.

articles.title: Die besten KI-Agenten machen den langweiligsten Job
articles.text:
Warum die spannendsten KI-Agenten ziemlich langweilige Aufgaben erledigen
Weniger Science-Fiction, mehr Geschäftsprozess
KI-Agenten sollen recherchieren, entscheiden, Software bedienen und ganze Aufgaben selbstständig erledigen. Die Vision klingt nach einem grundlegenden Wandel der Wissensarbeit. Doch wer Agentic AI im Unternehmen einsetzen will, steht zunächst vor einer viel pragmatischeren Frage: Bei welchen Aufgaben lohnt sich ein KI-Agent überhaupt?
Eine Antwort liefert die Telekom AI Agent-Studie 2026. Dafür wurden 123 KI-affine Entscheider*innen aus deutschen Unternehmen mit 50 bis 2.500 Mitarbeitenden befragt und 13 Anwendungsfälle für Agentic AI untersucht. Die Stichprobe ist bewusst kein repräsentativer Querschnitt des Mittelstands, sondern fokussiert Unternehmen mit höherer KI-Affinität.
Das Ergebnis ist weniger futuristisch, als der aktuelle Agenten-Hype vermuten lässt.
Der Sweet Spot liegt zwischen Einzelschritt und End-to-End-Automatisierung
Besonders interessant sind wiederkehrende Prozesse, die mehrere Arbeitsschritte und Systeme miteinander verbinden. Acht Anwendungsfälle wurden priorisiert: Auftrags- und Rechnungsverarbeitung, Angebotserstellung, E-Mail-Service, Einkauf und Beschaffung, Lead Research, telefonischer Service sowie IT-Support und Ticketbearbeitung.
Der Sweet Spot liegt bei zwei bis vier Systemen und zwei bis vier Prozessschritten. Für einzelne Aufgaben reicht häufig ein KI-Tool oder klassische Automatisierung. Hochkomplexe End-to-End-Prozesse sind dagegen schwieriger zu standardisieren. Agentic AI wird damit vor allem dort interessant, wo Menschen heute Systeme miteinander verbinden, Daten prüfen oder den nächsten Prozessschritt anstoßen.
Angebot, Auftrag, Rechnung: unspektakulär – aber relevant
Wie das aussehen kann, zeigt der Prozess vom Angebot bis zur Rechnung (wie hier am Beispiel Paula). Drei der priorisierten Anwendungsfälle bilden dabei eine Prozesskette: Angebotserstellung, Auftragsverarbeitung und Rechnungsverarbeitung. Ein Agent kann Informationen aus einer Kundenanfrage strukturieren und CRM-, Produkt- und Preisdaten für einen Angebotsentwurf zusammenführen. Bei der Auftragsverarbeitung können eingehende Bestellungen erfasst, mit Daten im Warenwirtschaftssystem abgeglichen und für die weitere Bearbeitung vorbereitet werden. In der Rechnungsverarbeitung lassen sich wiederum Dokumente erkennen, prüfen und in definierte Freigabeprozesse überführen. Bei Abweichungen oder kritischen Entscheidungen bleibt der Mensch in der Prüfschleife.
            
            
        
    
            Telekom MMS
    
      Telekom MMS unterstützt Unternehmen dabei, digitale Lösungen von der Strategie bis zum produktiven Betrieb umzusetzen. Im Bereich KI verbindet das Unternehmen Beratung, Entwicklung und Integration mit sicheren und skalierbaren Betriebsmodellen.
Dass solche systemübergreifenden Workflows auch in der Praxis funktionieren, zeigt die cec Ingenieurgesellschaft: Eine auf n8n basierende KI-Lösung automatisiert dort die Verarbeitung und Zuordnung von Fotodokumentationen aus Tiefbauprojekten und bindet bestehende Microsoft-Systeme ein.
Der wirtschaftliche Hebel liegt weniger im Agenten selbst als im Prozess: weniger manuelle Übertragungen, kürzere Bearbeitungszeiten und weniger Fehlerquellen. Vor dem Start sollte deshalb geklärt werden, wie häufig ein Vorgang anfällt, wie viel Aufwand heute entsteht und anhand welcher Kennzahlen die Wirkung später gemessen wird. Der ROI-Kompass für KI im Mittelstand unterscheidet drei Wirkungsfelder: Effizienz, Leistungsfähigkeit und Wachstum.
Damit aus langweiligen Aufgaben echter Mehrwert wird
Ein Agent allein macht noch keinen Geschäftsprozess. Damit aus einer Kundenanfrage ein Angebot, aus einer Bestellung ein Auftrag oder aus einer Rechnung ein verbuchter Vorgang wird, müssen Daten, Systeme und Regeln zusammenspielen. Damit wird Agentic AI auch zur Architektur- und Governance-Frage: Worauf darf ein Agent zugreifen? Was darf er selbst ausführen? Wann muss ein Mensch freigeben? Und wie bleiben Aktivitäten und Kosten transparent?
Genau hier setzt die T-AI Agent Platform an. Auf Basis von n8n verbindet sie Anwendungen, Datenquellen und Prozessschritte in Workflows. Die Plattform schafft Leitplanken für den produktiven Einsatz: Rollen und Berechtigungen, Freigaben, Monitoring und nachvollziehbare Aktivitäten sowie Transparenz über Nutzung und Kosten. Der Betrieb erfolgt dediziert bei der Telekom in Deutschland.
So können aus einzelnen Automatisierungen wiederverwendbare Workflows und weitere Anwendungen entstehen. Gerade in täglich wiederkehrenden Aufgaben liegt ein unterschätztes Potenzial: Nicht die spektakulärste KI-Anwendung muss den größten Unterschied machen, sondern die, die einen relevanten Prozess zuverlässig besser macht.
Die vermeintlich langweiligen Aufgaben könnten dafür ein ziemlich guter Anfang sein.

articles.title: WeatherNext 3, el modelo con IA que predice fenómenos atmosféricos con mucha más precisión
articles.text: Representación gráfica de las nubes, similar a una imagen analizada por WeatherNext 3, el modelo de predicción meteorológica con inteligencia artificial de Google DeepMind. El equipo de Google DeepMind ha desarrollado WeatherNext 3 , un modelo de predicción meteorológica con inteligencia artificial (IA), lanzado el 3 de septiembre, que incorpora directamente datos observados de la atmósfera, incluidos datos de satélites y estaciones meteorológicas. Frente a modelos anteriores de predicción meteorológica con inteligencia artificial, como GraphCast , WeatherNext 3 aumenta la resolución, de 28 kilómetros a cinco en algunas variables, lo que permite hacer predicciones en cuadrículas de hasta cinco por cinco kilómetros y ofrecer una representación más detallada de las condiciones atmosféricas, además de aumentar la frecuencia de sus previsiones, de seis horas a una, e incorporar observaciones directas de la atmósfera, como las imágenes satelitales. Ferran Alet Puig, investigador de Google DeepMind, explica cómo se han hecho tradicionalmente los pronósticos: “Lo que se hacía hasta ahora era estimar el tiempo lo mejor posible en el presente y predecir el futuro mediante la simulación de las ecuaciones de la física con parámetros estimados”. Su compañero, Álvaro Sánchez González, señala el cambio que introduce WeatherNext 3: “Permite al modelo de predicción acceder directamente a datos de la atmósfera que no son estimados, sino medidos”. articles.title: Calian and Invest Ottawa to open new defence research and development lab | BetaKit
articles.text:
An 1,850-acre research and development complex in Canada’s capital is getting a new defence tech lab.
The news: At GCXpo last week, Ottawa-based defence company Calian and regional innovation hub Invest Ottawa announced they will open the Northstar Defence Lab at Area X.O, an expansive R&D complex located in the city’s west end.
The Northstar Defence Lab is meant to be a “system-of-systems orchestration lab” that connects tech developed by different companies for different platforms and missions using Calian’s Athora platform. Athora allows the tech to securely share data, coordinate, and operate as an integrated system of systems.
From the source: Calian’s president of defence and space, Chris Pogue, told the Ottawa Business Journal last week that future defence tech will include fewer “monolithic systems” and more platforms built by different, specialized suppliers that adapt and change alongside the battlefield.
“It’s the idea that you have to rapidly innovate on the battlefield today, go back in your garage tonight, change it, and operate that way tomorrow morning,” Pogue said. “Northstar lab is designed to optimize Canadian industry to do that rapid cycle.”
The context: Calian and industry partners will contribute communications, data integration, AI, cybersecurity, sensing, and operational decision support resources to the lab. The founding partners include local defence firms like ADGA, Anvil, Larus, and Tactiql, as well as other Canadian companies like Evertz Microsystems, Tessellate Robotics, 123 Cyber, and Cohere, with federal agency Export Development Canada participating as an industry commercialization partner.
Calian said the lab is the first facility in its planned nationwide network of regional defence development labs, and that it is related to its $100-million push to advance Canada’s sovereign C5ISRT capabilities. C5ISRT stands for Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Cyber, Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance, and Targeting.
Final thought: As a certified test centre for NATO DIANA, the alliance’s defence tech accelerator program, Area X.O already has plenty of defence companies making use of its space. One such company is Victoria-based InDro Robotics, which has most of its staff in Ottawa because of the test site.
Area X.O sports advanced communications infrastructure and real-world urban and rural mobility infrastructure along 16 kilometres of test track, a designated drone area, and other resources for robot testing. Pogue told the Ottawa Business Journal that Calian is constructing the new building at Area X.O and expects it to be ready early next year.
Feature image courtesy Calian.

articles.title: Décès suspect en Sibérie : pourquoi la peste est-elle encore étudiée en 2026 ?
articles.text:
Une technicienne d’un laboratoire russe spécialisé dans la peste est morte le 1er octobre 2026, peut-être après avoir contracté la maladie qu’elle étudiait. Selon le média indépendant en exil Lioudi Baïkala, cité par l’AFP, Daria Chipilova était une technicienne de laboratoire de 28 ans, travaillant pour l’Institut anti-peste d’Irkoutsk. Elle avait été hospitalisée le 29 septembre avec des symptômes de pneumonie sévère, et son décès est survenu deux jours plus tard.
Daria Chipilova aurait brisé par accident un tube à essai contenant la bactérie de la peste, et aurait ainsi pu contracter la forme pulmonaire de la maladie. Près de 200 personnes ayant pu être en contact avec elle ont été placées sous surveillance médicale, dont plus d’une centaine à l’hôpital.
Cette suspicion autour d’une fuite de peste en laboratoire peut paraître inquiétante. Elle ne doit pas pour autant faire oublier ce qu’est réellement la peste. Contrairement à une croyance répandue, la peste n’a jamais disparu. Ce cas ne signifie donc pas que la maladie ferait son retour.
La peste, une zoonose qui a décimé l’Europe au Moyen Âge
La peste est une zoonose, qui se transmet principalement par la puce infectée par la bactérie Yersinia pestis. La puce peut être véhiculée par de petits animaux, notamment des rongeurs : s’ils sont au contact d’humains, ils peuvent les exposer à cette puce, et donc à la maladie en cas de piqure. En l’absence de traitement, la peste tue de 30 à 100 % des malades, selon la forme de la maladie.
La maladie est connue pour les ravages qu’elle a provoqués au Moyen Âge, avec la « mort noire » qui a sévi au milieu du 14e siècle, tuant entre 30 et 60 % de la population européenne. Après ce choc démographique, d’autres vagues épidémiques se sont produites pendant les siècles suivants, contribuant à donner à la peste cette image d’une maladie moyen-âgeuse dévastratrice, avant que l’on comprenne mieux son fonctionnement au gré des progrès de la médecine.
Aujourd’hui, la peste n’est pas éradiquée
La peste a pourtant survécu au Moyen Âge. « Quoique la peste ne soit plus de nos jours le fléau qu’elle a été par le passé, grâce en particulier à la découverte de l’agent causal, du cycle de transmission, et surtout grâce à l’utilisation de traitements antibiotiques efficaces, elle est loin d’avoir été éradiquée », expliquaient ainsi en 2008 les chercheuses Françoise Guinet et Elisabeth Carniel de l’Institut Pasteur.
Entre 1990 et 2020, près de 50 000 cas de peste ont été déclarés à l’OMS par 26 pays, selon l’Institut Pasteur. La maladie sévit principalement en Afrique, en Asie et en Amérique (en France, les derniers cas remontent à 1945, en Corse) et « fait partie des maladies actuellement ré-émergentes dans le monde ». Grâce à l’usage des antibiotiques (efficaces s’ils sont administrés rapidement) et aux mesures de santé publique, la mortalité a fortement baissé au cours du 20e siècle.
D’ailleurs, « une des caractéristiques des épidémies de peste est leur capacité à ‘s’éteindre’ pendant plusieurs années avant de réapparaître brutalement sous forme épidémique », souligne l’Institut Pasteur. Ainsi, en 1994, l’Inde a connu une épidémie de peste pulmonaire, alors que l’on pensait la maladie éradiquée depuis presque 30 ans. La Russie elle-même a vu réapparaître des cas humains en 2013, après 34 ans d’absence. Il est donc nécessaire de continuer à étudier de près cette maladie, et de ne pas la considérer comme appartenant au passé.
Aucun vaccin efficace et sûr contre la peste
Il n’existe à ce jour aucun vaccin sûr et efficace contre la peste, et les traitements utilisés ont parfois leurs limites. Françoise Guinet et Elisabeth Carniel ont ainsi relevé que le bacille pesteux, Yersinia pestis, peut développer dans certains cas une résistance aux antibiotiques utilisés pour le traitement de la peste. Ces antibiotiques restent une solution pour guérir la maladie, mais la possibilité d’une émergence de souches du bacille résistantes doit être surveillée, car elle constituerait « une menace majeure en santé publique ».
Françoise Guinet et Elisabeth Carniel résument ainsi : « La peste ne se présente plus aujourd’hui sous la forme des épidémies massives et dévastatrices qui ont marqué l’histoire et la mémoire collective des hommes. Cependant, cette maladie pose encore au monde actuel d’importants défis. » Sa gravité et sa contagiosité obligent encore aujourd’hui à réagir vite au moindre début d’épidémie. La panique que provoque la maladie pose aussi problème, car elle peut pousser des populations à fuir et propager ainsi la peste. La peste peut aussi se manifester de nouveau là où on ne l’observait plus, si bien que « l’éradication d’un foyer de peste établi ne peut jamais être tenue pour acquise ».
Des foyers naturels restent actifs sur plusieurs continents, et des établissements comme l’Institut anti-peste d’Irkoutsk servent justement à étudier les agents pathogènes dangereux de Sibérie et d’Extrême-Orient. Pour la jeune technicienne d’Irkoutsk, aucun diagnostic de peste n’a été confirmé publiquement. L’agence sanitaire russe Rospotrebnadzor affirme même n’avoir retrouvé dans ses prélèvements aucun des agents pathogènes de son laboratoire, sans dire pour autant de quoi elle est morte.

articles.title: Can Safeworld convince people that GenAI robots won't hurt them? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The big trend in robots is handing the keys over to a generative AI model, but that brings with it a problem: that architecture isn’t predictable the way traditional algorithms are. How can you be sure your brand new humanoid will be safe?
Dr. Ding Zhao, who directs the Safe AI lab at Carnegie Mellon University, has been working on this problem for almost his entire career. Now, along with veteran startup executive Kyle Wong and machine learning engineer Simo Rachidi, he’s founded a company, Safeworld, intended to solve it.
“The safety challenge that we’re talking about is a combination of, one, really advanced generative AI probabilistic evals — how do you underwrite the risk of a probabilistic system?” Zhao says. “The second part that’s really hard is the trust part, and you need both to deploy a robot.”
Safeworld is emerging from stealth today with a seed round of more than $12 million, led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun, with additional investment from Box Group, Carnegie Mellon University Endowment, Innovation Endeavors and SV Angel.
“The time to build an industry safety standard is now while robots are being designed and deployed,” a16z Speedrun partner Jonathan Lai told TechCurnch. “By the time you have robots in households colliding with kids and causing safety incidents, that’s way too late.”
Safeworld’s specialty is evaluating a robotic control system in simulations that are populated with realistic human models. It’s akin to the challenge faced by companies like Tesla or Wayve, which must ensure that their vehicles respond appropriately to a variety of surprising incidents they may encounter on the road. But that will be more difficult for robots, Zhao argues, because they work in unstructured environments, and because each facility they are in will have different safety standards.
“One of the most common areas is if there is a blind corner in this particular factory,” Wong said. “What is the speed or what is the stopping distance that you need to make sure that this robot will not collide with a particular human? If a human is carrying boxes, for example, will the robot detect the human or not?”
To answer that question, Safeworld will build a digital version of that corner in a model like Genesis or MuJoCo, insert a simulation of the robot it is evaluating, driven by its real software, and then run thousands of scenarios where human models encounter the robot. That’s harder than it seems, per Zhao, because people are unpredictable.
“Tripping and falling is also a good example of something that we do a lot of testing with the simulation,” Wong said. “Otherwise, you would have to go and trip and fall for the robot, which is like a hard thing to be doing all the time.”
There are definite similarities between the platform that Safeworld is building and the tools being used internally by robot builders. The founders, however, believe that beyond their specific expertise, robot-makers will want a third-party to validate their work, if only to share information about safety cases between competitors.
“A lot of people are underestimating how hard some of these edge cases are going to be to solve,” Zhao said. “It is not the robot in the vacuum, in the demo, that we are worried about. It is the robot that is deployed at scale, with people who potentially never operated a robot before.”
Vishal Dugar, the CTO of Gritt Robotics, is developing the AI brain for robots that currently help workers install photovoltaic panels at industrial-scale solar farms, and aspires to take on more complex construction tasks. His company is partnering with Safeworld as they develop their safety simulations.
“The difficulty with most of our systems is it’s very hard to formally prove it by doing some math, writing some equations, and saying yeah, the system is verified to be safe,” Dugar says. “It necessarily has to be done empirically.”
His robots operate alongside human workers, and ensuring that a robotic arm doesn’t hit them is obviously top of mind. To verify that in practice requires considering all kinds of potential scenarios.
“Humans have many kinds of appearances,” Dugar points out. “Their bodies can be in different configurations. They could be kneeling, standing. They could be tripping and falling potentially. They could be crouching. They could be running. You have to respond to all these behaviors that humans could potentially exhibit on these sites, along with the variety of variations in human appearance, you know, clothes, size, shape, height, skin color, everything else.”
It’s still early days for both Safeworld and generative AI in robotics, and the company is still figuring out the best model for its product — a platform for external users, or a services-based approach? — but the team is confident they are taking on the right problem.
“We’ll probably be the first profitable company in this field,” Zaho says. “Because if anyone wants to deploy, they need to pay us to handle the situation.”

articles.title: Downgrading user roles in Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Downgrading user roles in Amazon Quick
Managing access permissions effectively is an important aspect of maintaining a secure and collaborative environment in Amazon Quick. Quick supports versatile user management options designed to accommodate various identity types and organizational needs. You can provision users natively through Quick Identity or manage them through enterprise identity providers such as AWS IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. These systems allow user roles including Admin, Author, and Reader to be assigned and grouped according to job functions and security requirements. As team members join, change roles, or leave the organization, administrators must make sure transitions happen smoothly without disrupting business workflows or creating security gaps.
Regular access reviews are important for maintaining security in your Quick environment. Plan monthly or quarterly audits of user roles to confirm everyone has appropriate permissions. When team members’ responsibilities change, proactively transfer ownership of their dashboards and analyses to prevent orphaned resources. This practice, recommended in the AWS Well-Architected Framework, helps maintain continuity for business-critical visualizations.
In this post, we focus on one specific but important user lifecycle task: downgrading user roles.
Why downgrade?
The principle of least privilege applies strongly to Quick administration. Users should have access only to what they need for their specific job functions. Downgrading user roles is a key part of enforcing least privilege. When a user’s responsibilities no longer require authoring or administrative capabilities, reduce their role accordingly to minimize the security surface area.
Quick pricing is also role-based: Authors and Admins pay a fixed monthly per-user fee, while Readers use session-based pricing. Organizations with users provisioned as Authors who only consume dashboards can reduce costs substantially by right-sizing them to Reader roles. For current pricing details, see the Amazon Quick pricing page.
For more granular control beyond the built-in roles in Amazon Quick, consider complementing role assignments with Custom Permissions, which restrict specific capabilities within a role tier. The integration of Amazon Quick with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) provides additional permission boundaries that complement the basic role system.
Scope of this post
Although the exact steps depend on the user identity type, this post primarily addresses Amazon Quick Identity users (also called Quick-managed users). Users authenticated through IAM Identity Center or Active Directory typically have role changes managed through their external identity provider group mappings. If your environment uses IAM Identity Center, role downgrade is handled by moving the user from one IdC group to another (for example, from a Quick-Admins group to a Quick-Readers group). No step-down sequence is required.
Although the Amazon Quick console doesn’t provide a direct downgrade path for all role transitions (specifically, you cannot downgrade from Admin to Reader or from Author to Reader directly through the console interface), two reliable solutions exist: a manual deletion-and-recreation method, and an approach that uses the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). We walk you through both techniques to help you maintain proper access management as your team evolves.
Prerequisites
Before we begin, make sure you have an active AWS account with administrator access to Amazon Quick. If you plan to use the CLI method, you need the AWS CLI installed and configured on your machine. It’s also helpful to prepare a list of users whose roles need changing.
Understanding Amazon Quick roles
Amazon Quick offers two subscription tiers with distinct role sets:
| Subscription | Roles | Capabilities | 
| Amazon Quick Enterprise | Admin Pro, Author Pro, Reader Pro | Full BI + AI features (agents, topics, Q&A, stories, generative summaries) | 
| Amazon Quick Sight (BI-only) | Admin, Author, Reader | Traditional BI authoring and consumption | 
The console does not provide a direct way to downgrade from any Author tier to any Reader tier. The update-user API enforces this same constraint, rejecting direct downgrades with a “You cannot downgrade a user role” error.
The following screenshot shows the Amazon Quick Suite user management page, where the console offers no direct control to move a user from an Author tier down to a Reader tier. This illustrates why the methods in this post are necessary.
The CLI step-down method works reliably for the legacy BI-only roles (Admin, Author, Reader), following this sequence:
Admin > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader
This same sequence also works for Pro users, as long as the intermediate steps use the legacy roles. For example, Author Pro > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader Pro completes successfully.
Important considerations before making changes
When implementing role changes through either method, there are several important factors to keep in mind. First, verify that all users in your list are currently Admin or Author users before making changes. Attempting to downgrade users who already have lower permissions might cause errors. Resource ownership questions still apply even when using the CLI method. Users being downgraded will no longer be able to edit resources they previously owned. For larger organizations using the CLI method, consider loading user email addresses from a CSV file rather than hardcoding them. If you use AWS CloudShell instead of a local CLI installation, you can omit the AWS Region specification because AWS CloudShell automatically uses your current console Region context.
Transferring asset ownership (do this first)
Before deleting a user, it’s essential to make sure that any assets they own, such as dashboards, datasets, and analyses, are properly reassigned. This prevents disruptions and avoids leaving resources orphaned. If the user is an Author, verify whether they own any datasets or dashboards, and follow the same asset reassignment steps described here. There are three main ways to handle asset ownership transfers in Amazon Quick.
Option 1: Proactively transfer ownership to another admin
The most controlled approach is to manually reassign ownership before deleting the user. To do this, go into each asset in Quick, choose Share, and assign another admin as a co-owner. With this method, you can determine exactly who takes over each resource, which is especially useful for high-impact dashboards or datasets. Although this can be time-consuming in large environments, it gives you the flexibility to distribute assets according to your team’s structure and responsibilities.
The following screenshot shows the Share dialog for an asset, where you add another admin as a co-owner so that ownership is transferred before the original user is removed.
Option 2: Use the Amazon Quick bulk asset transfer on the Admin page
If the user owns many assets, the manual method can become inefficient. In this case, you can use the Manage assets feature available in the Admin section of Quick. With this tool, administrators can perform bulk ownership transfers or update sharing permissions for multiple assets at once. It streamlines the reassignment process significantly, particularly when offboarding users or managing organizational changes. For more details on how to use this feature, see the official Managing assets in Amazon Quick documentation.
Option 3: Share assets with a Quick user group
Another effective strategy is to share assets with a user group. For Quick Identity users, you can create a Quick group, add relevant team members, and share dashboards or datasets with the group rather than individual users. If your account is integrated with IAM Identity Center or Active Directory, equivalent groups are created and managed in those systems, and Quick uses those external groups for access control instead of Quick-managed groups. This way, access to shared resources remains intact even if a specific user is deleted. It’s a resilient approach that reduces the need for reassigning ownership in the future and helps maintain consistent access across dynamic teams.
Manual method: Deleting and recreating the user
Although not the most efficient approach, the manual deletion and recreation method is one option for environments where CLI usage isn’t feasible. This method involves removing the admin user entirely and then recreating them with reader permissions. This same manual method also applies when downgrading an Author to a Reader, though typically with fewer complications around asset ownership.
Because this method requires deleting the user account before recreating it with a lower role, careful preparation is essential to avoid losing valuable resources and disrupting workflows. Make sure you have completed the asset ownership transfer described in the previous section before proceeding.
Step 1: Delete the admin user
After you transfer ownership of all resources, sign in to the AWS Management Console and navigate to the Amazon Quick service. From there, choose your profile icon, and then choose Manage Quick, followed by Manage users. When you locate the admin user you want to downgrade, choose the delete icon next to their name and confirm the deletion when prompted. This completely removes their current access to the system.
If you haven’t transferred all resources beforehand, Quick presents an ownership transfer dialog. This dialog prompts you to select another admin who will receive ownership of all the user’s resources. Select an appropriate admin from the list, then confirm the transfer by choosing Delete and transfer. This built-in transfer mechanism helps prevent orphaned resources but transfers everything to a single admin. For more granular control, use the proactive approach mentioned earlier to distribute resources strategically among different team members.
If you skipped the proactive transfer, the deletion dialog shown in the following figure lets you reassign all of the user’s resources to a single admin before the account is removed.
Step 2: Recreate the user with the Reader role
After successfully deleting the user, remain on the Users page and choose Invite users. Enter the user’s email address and select the Reader role from the available options. Send the invitation to allow the user to rejoin Quick with their new, more restricted permissions.
Step 3: Verify the role change
After the user accepts the invitation:
- Confirm that their permissions have been updated to Reader.
- Verify that they can only view dashboards and reports.
- Confirm that they can’t modify or create content.
CLI method: Step-down role transition (recommended)
If you prefer to use the AWS CLI or AWS CloudShell, you can programmatically change the user’s role. Because Quick requires role changes to be made in a specific sequence, you can’t transition directly from any Admin to any Reader. Instead, you must step through intermediate roles.
Important notes
- Replace <your-account-id> with your AWS account ID.
- Replace <user-name> with the username of the user.
- Replace <user-email> with the user’s email address.
- If you’re using the AWS CLI outside CloudShell, specify the --region parameter.
- The --role value must match the API role name exactly (see the preceding table).
Example: Legacy track (Admin to Reader)
Step 1: Change role from Admin to Author:
Step 2: Update role from Author to Restricted Reader:
Step 3: Change role from Restricted Reader to Reader:
After the downgrade: Review Limit Profiles and Custom Permissions
Role changes don’t automatically adjust Limit Profiles or Custom Permissions profiles. Both persist independently of the user’s role, and you should review them after any downgrade.
- Limit Profiles control per-user caps on resources such as index storage and agent hours. If the downgraded user was assigned a profile appropriate for their previous Admin or Author role, reassign a Reader-appropriate limit profile to avoid over-allocating resources. See the Limit Profiles documentation for details.
- Custom Permissions restrict specific capabilities within a role tier. A profile assigned to an Author might not behave as expected on a Reader. Either unapply it during the final CLI step (using --unapply-custom-permissions) or assign a profile designed for the Reader tier.
Script for updating multiple users
Use the following script to update multiple users.
Script functionality
This script performs the following:
- Reads usernames and email addresses from an external file (supports comments with #).
- Updates role in three stages: Admin > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader.
- Error handling stops the transition for a user if any step fails.
- Sleep commands allow time for changes to take effect.
A few things to keep in mind when running the script:
- Confirm users are currently Admin or Author users before running.
- Use the actual Quick username, which might differ from the email prefix in federated environments.
- No Region specification needed in AWS CloudShell.
- You can modify the script to load users from a CSV export of list-users.
Best practices for user access management
To keep your Quick environment secure and well-organized, follow these best practices:
- Review user roles regularly (monthly or quarterly audits).
- Transfer resource ownership before changing roles.
- Follow the principle of least privilege.
- Use Custom Permissions profiles for fine-grained control within a role tier.
- Share resources with groups rather than individuals for resilience.
- Use AWS Identity and Access Management for additional permission boundaries.
Cleaning up
After completing user role changes:
- Remove any test users.
- Verify that no unintended resources remain.
- Delete temporary CLI scripts or user list files.
- Double-check the final user permissions.
Conclusion
In this post, we explored two methods to downgrade user roles in Amazon Quick: manual deletion and recreation, and a flexible AWS CLI approach. These strategies help you manage team access efficiently and securely.
For environments using IAM Identity Center, role changes are managed through IdC group reassignment, which does not require the step-down sequence described here. For additional governance controls, explore Custom Permissions for feature-level restrictions and Restricted Folders for content-level isolation.
Resources
We’d love to hear about your user management experiences. How does your organization handle role transitions in Quick Suite? Have you developed custom scripts or processes to streamline these changes? Share your thoughts and challenges in the comments.

articles.text:
Le top 3 des meilleurs modèles sur Frandroid

Mova S70 Ultra Roller

La fin d’année est l’occasion idéale de refaire son équipement pour gérer et nettoyer son domicile. Dans notre sélection des meilleurs robots aspirateurs, vous trouverez des références parmi les plus performantes du marché. Lors du mois de septembre qui vient de s’écouler, nous avons testé plusieurs modèles. Quels sont ceux qui ont retenu notre attention ? Au programme de ce top 3, un DJI, un Mova et un Dreame.
La référence
- Cartographie et évitement d'obstacles toujours au sommet, objets transparents et câbles fins compris
- La puissance enfin au niveau : tapis épais, rainures de parquet et taches incrustées maîtrisés
- Des jambes robotisées qui franchissent jusqu'à 8,5 cm, du jamais vu chez nous
- Le bras oscillant de 123° qui lave sous les meubles et au ras des plinthes
- Une station annoncée pour un an sans entretien, et un silence remarquable
- Un tarif premium de 1 299 € qui réserve le P2 à une minorité
- Le design transparent, que nous adorons, ne fera pas l'unanimité
- L'assistant vocal « OK ROMO » indisponible dans certains pays au lancement
- Le mode Données locales seulement annoncé pour fin 2026
- L'historique logiciel de la première génération nous incite à rester vigilant sur les promesses de mises à jour
Le DJI Romo P2 est sans nul doute la nouvelle référence de notre guide d’achat des meilleurs aspirateurs robots. Le modèle reprend le design tout en transparence de la génération précédente. Au quotidien, le nettoyage s’adapte automatiquement à ce que le robot détecte : il augmente l’aspiration sur les tapis et traite à part les liquides renversés. Côté performances, le Romo P2 revendique une puissance d’aspiration maximale de 36 000 Pa, qui lui permet de ramasser les débris, y compris sur les tapis et textiles. Pour ce qui est du lavage humide, il se dote de patins rotatifs très efficaces. Un bras articulé, qui pivote jusqu’à 123°, lui permet d’atteindre les coins et les pieds de meubles. DJI annonce jusqu’à 365 jours sans entretien pour la station, dans ses propres conditions de test. Lancé à 1 299 euros, il se trouve déjà à 1 059 euros chez plusieurs revendeurs : cela reste un réel investissement.
L'aspirateur laveur abordable
Le Mova S70 Ultra Roller est la preuve d’une vraie amélioration du constructeur sur le sujet des aspirateurs robots. D’abord grâce à un design retravaillé avec une station esthétique aux belles finitions. L’application Mova qui accompagne le robot est complète, avec toutes les fonctions attendues. Il dispose d’un mode CleanGenius qui permet au robot d’ajuster son nettoyage selon la saleté détectée. Pour ce qui est du nettoyage, le Mova S70 Ultra Roller dispose d’une puissance d’aspiration à 32 000 Pa. Ce qui est suffisant pour la plupart des sols et tapis. Le lavage passe par un rouleau de serpillère avec de l’eau chaude jusqu’à 100 °C. En 3 h 30 de nettoyage, l’aspirateur couvre 120 m². La navigation est efficace avec une bonne détection d’obstacles. Un dernier mot sur l’entretien qui reste assez simple au quotidien. Avec un prix officiel de 699 euros, c’est un aspirateur robot que nous pouvons vous conseiller sans réfléchir.
Le Dreame L50s Pro Ultra se positionne en milieu de gamme, avec des fondamentaux solides. Son design est élégant avec un format compact tout en verticalité. L’application compagnon DreameHome est intuitive. Celle-ci offre toutes les fonctionnalités attendues comme la fusion de pièces ou la création de zones interdites à l’aspirateur. Le nettoyage de l’aspirateur robot est convaincant avec une puissance d’aspiration à 30 000 Pa et des patins rotatifs. En revanche, la navigation montre ses limites : le L50s Pro Ultra s’entête parfois contre certains obstacles. La détection des taches est elle aussi parfois décevante. L’entretien de la machine est quasi minimaliste avec peu d’intervention humaine nécessaire. Lancé à 749 euros, il se trouve aujourd’hui autour de 600 euros : à ce prix, c’est un modèle intéressant si vous souhaitez une machine fiable sans trop dépenser.

articles.title: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
articles.text:
Orbital data centers, defense systems, quantum computing, particle physics, and advanced manufacturing are raising the bar for simulation, test, and lab tools.
Key Takeaways:
Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once. Radiation, thermal shock, vibration, pressure, noise, and cryogenic temperatures are colliding in applications ranging from orbital data centers and defense systems to particle physics, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing.
That is changing how chips are designed and qualified. AI-enabled design tools, machine learning, and language models can explore more design options earlier, but virtual models still have to be checked against physical behavior. For extreme-environment electronics, the challenge is not just predicting failure modes, but reproducing enough of the real operating environment to trust the prediction.
Space is becoming one of the clearest pressure points. The growth of satellite constellations, orbital data centers, space probes, surface explorers, and military space systems is increasing demand for radiation-hardened designs, including at newer process nodes where performance and power benefits must be balanced against survivability. That demand is already showing up in the design ecosystem.
“We have seen a major uptick in activity for rad-hard fab processes, particularly in the new process nodes to support orbital data centers,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “A lot of this is owing to the Golden Dome (multi-layered U.S. missile defense initiative). The next frontier for the next battlefield is space, and so you’re seeing the investment now accelerate, and we’re going to see a lot more rad-hard designs added.”
Beyond national security, governments and nations are competing for global leadership in emerging technologies.
For example, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) is working with Morgan State University, Northrop Grumman, and Project Omega on the DARPA-funded Rads to Watts program, which aims to convert Cold War-era radioactive decay into high-density nuclear micro-power radiovoltaic systems for extreme environments, including space, remote sensing, undersea infrastructure, and defense applications. [1]
Radioisotopes such as Strontium-90 will be converted directly into electricity to operate for decades without refueling or battery replacement. Researchers achieve this by combining ultra-thin semiconductor layers with high-energy, beta-emitting isotopes. Simulation, characterization, and survivability analysis are essential to ensure these systems can operate in harsh environments.
Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory is working with Siemens on a project titled Accelerating eXtreme Environment Specs-to-Silicon (AXESS) that uses LLMs and smaller surrogate models to speed up design exploration, then integrate and co-optimize all stages of chip development for quantum computing, fusion energy, and particle physics. [2]
Fig. 1: A Fermilab engineer holds a custom circuit board designed to measure chip performance in cryogenic environments. Source: JJ Starr/Fermilab
Each extreme-environment application presents a unique set of physical stressors that the hardware device must account for.
“Particle accelerators and research accelerators are a particularly challenging environment because the doses are ridiculously high, and you need the equipment to do its thing while it’s getting damaged by the radiation,” said Hugh Barnaby, leader of extreme environment reliability in the U.S. Department of Defense’s ME Commons SWAP Hub at Arizona State University. “That extends to the medical equipment that’s used in proton therapies for cancer, which uses high-energy electrons. And in semiconductor manufacturing, lithography causes radiation damage. They’re using X-rays now for some of the really advanced technology, like backside power delivery. They have the power distribution on the backside of the chip. They used to use a wafer-analysis technique called LADA (laser-assisted device alteration), but now they can’t because the power is on the backside. They can’t use the lights. So they’re considering X-ray-assisted device alteration lasers (XADA). The problem is, they’re worried about the X-rays causing damage to the material.”
Barnaby and one of his students, Jereme Neuendank, found that strange things happen to semiconductors at very low temperatures. [3] “If you combine that with radiation, it gets even weirder,” said Barnaby. ” We had some good theories with models backing them up, and we’re still doing a lot of work in that area.”
Lab tools are evolving to study the effects of multiple stressors at once. ASU researchers developed the Rigel DSTAT, which has three rods collectively containing 9,000 Curies (Ci) of radioactive material to simulate the radiation environments found in space and nuclear applications. It also contains a tiny cryostat, which enables devices to be exposed to really saturated, extremely cold temperatures by evacuating a chamber and then filling it with either liquid nitrogen or argon, whose temperatures are about the same. “Then we can do radiation testing at liquid nitrogen, which is 77 Kelvin,” said Barnaby.
Fig. 2: This illustrated setup shows how ASU’s extreme environments lab would test radiation and extreme cold together to mimic space. Illustration by Sophia Franz. Source: ASU
The tool was ideal for a company designing readout ICs for satellites that would need to withstand cold, radiation, ionizing-dose threats, and low-frequency noise. In particular, random telegraph noise has emerged as one of the biggest reliability problems today, especially in analog/mixed-signal electronics. And that noise problem is exacerbated in the cold.
“You want the cold to reduce the noise that comes off of the diodes that are creating the currents, the light detectors,” Barnaby noted. “They like the cold there. But when you’re doing the CMOS, to do the readout of those signals, the random telegraph noise signal does not, at best, improve with cold temperature. We’re still studying that physics.”
The applications for these kinds of lab tools are growing. “We have talked to people about doing research in thermal energy exploration,” he explained. “We’ve also been getting into advanced packaging, which means extending into a pretty wide array of reliability issues such as pressure, humidity, high temperature — not just low — as well as radiation, thermal shock, mechanical shock, and vibration. We’re working with NXP quite a bit these days at their facility in Phoenix.”
Simulating electronics for space
Extreme environments such as space benefit from a 4D geospatial model and digital twin, which can include thermal and radiation data.
“If something gets hot, we can tell you how much the component stretches or shrinks or stresses,” said Shawn Carpenter, program director for 5G/6G and space at Synopsys, who recently worked with NASA on lunar network propagation. [4] “You can see whether the materials align and work properly. Thermal is a really big one for us because of the extremes that equipment goes through from direct illumination to shadow from the sun.”
Another stressor is that, in outer space, thermal cycling can range from -40°F to 120°F in the same day. “Your mean time to first failure is much higher,” said Lang Lin, director of product management at Synopsys. “We want to keep temperatures down because we want a very long lifetime for the electronics. But in outer space, when you have this thermal cycling changing so fast, it decreases the lifetime.” Then you add radiation. “All of our transistors here on Earth have a certain limited tolerance to radiation. But when you go to outer space, all the neutrons and protons and electrons from the sun go into the oxide of the transistors, and that messes up their performance.”
Designers need to build chips that support the particular mission. “We try to shorten the time it takes for someone to build a very capable chipset by providing them with IP for whatever target,” said Carpenter. “For example, the smaller nodes are highly desirable for the power that they’re going to save. We need to model the physics of that chip in operation. How hot does it get? Does it maintain signal integrity? How does it age? How long will it last? Will signals bleed into other parts of the package? Then there are integration questions. If I put that chip in a package, how does it perform? If I put that package on a carrier board, how does that perform? If I put it inside of a module, how do I get the heat out? How can I conduct that heat effectively? What are my power requirements?”
Simulation tools can answer all of those questions quickly. “If suddenly TSMC comes out with a 1.5nm process and you say, ‘Okay, I’m going to save 30% power by going to that new node, let’s go get the blocks, let’s re-spin the chip, let’s rebuild this stuff before we go out for the next mission,’ then we build that out to the system evaluation,” he said. “How does the chip work, as informed by where you’re operating it, how you’re using it, and the cycles it’s going to go through for heating and whatever else the environment throws at it?”
For space applications, physics questions need to be answered in the context of a large, gravitationally informed environment where things swirl at incredible speeds.
Simulation, digital twinning, and AI-enabled tools can be combined to model objects, people, and systems in orbit or on the lunar surface. “You don’t want that data spoofed, so that the location is actually different than what you think it is,” Neustadter warned.
Agentic AI will also be part of the equation. “Especially when you start talking about militaristic functionality — vehicles that are going to be more like a drone, in the use case of an orbital communications hub or orbital lab, these vehicles are going to need to be mobile, they’re going to need to react, they’re going to have weapon systems on them,” said Neustadter. “We know there are nuclear warheads already up there, and that’s part of how we destroy or circumvent them.”
AI doesn’t always enhance safety, but it increases adaptability. Neustadter noted that if you lose control of a vehicle, it should be autonomous most of the time and able to learn and transmit data. Since communication costs are high at the desired data rates, it’s beneficial to handle some processing locally and only send the critical information back.
Counteracting radiation 
Many military components already are prepared for a nuclear event in space, which disrupts the electromagnetic pulses (EMP) of all the electronics.
“The military has to have protection against EMP and high-altitude EMP (HEMP),” said Lin. “Military airplanes require extremely expensive shielding and grounding techniques that are not required for commercial aviation and some of the electronics we have today. But for space applications, that’s required, and it’s more expensive. DO-160 EMC certification requirements are more for aerospace. Whenever you have an EMP, and that could be because of a nuclear reaction or sun storms, you have a potential issue with your electronics. If the electronics aren’t strong enough, the EMP will generate some inrush current, and you’re going to have to reset your computer.”
After a reset, EMP-induced excess current can damage semiconductors. “Then you’re going to have to replace it,” Lin said. “It depends on the EMP level and the protection needed. Currently, no data centers here on Earth have EMP protection, but space-based ones will likely need specialized shielding, which would raise development costs for orbital data centers.
On Earth, AI data centers and automotive systems need less protection from atmospheric radiation than in space, but single event upsets caused by unusual sun activity and cosmic rays are still a concern.
“Cosmic rays cause bit flips and other random events, which can be catastrophic for the AI training run, and then for inference as well, for running the AI workloads,” said Matthew Bubis, director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “You may have voting systems, for example. You might have more than one GPU and a system for comparing their outputs. Then, inside each GPU, you have checks that take place, which we do in automotive as well, to determine whether an event like an upset or a bit flip has occurred. Then we can detect and correct those transient events. There’s a lot of commonality with automotive. It’s just that there are more of these events up in space, and the consequences are different. It’s not a safety consequence. It’s a reliability issue. Are you going to get the output that you’re looking for if there are these constant bit flips going on?”
Many automotive-grade safety features can help components withstand space conditions. “Our IP has built-in reliability features,” Bubis noted. “The chipmaker handles the radiation hardening side, and then even beyond that, someone else supports the system with radiation protection, which goes around the chip. Space needs this multi-layered approach to the designs.”
While orbital data centers are leveraging sun-synchronous solar power for now, nuclear-powered micro reactors like those being developed by DARPA’s Rads to Watts program could benefit deep space propulsion, lunar and Martian surface bases, and intensive activity such as in-orbit manufacturing.
“A nuclear reactor is basically some nuclear material, with nuclear rods that contain nuclear particles, usually plutonium or something similar,” said Helmut Puchner, fellow and vice president of Aerospace and Defense at Infineon Technologies. “That’s the fuel. That material is highly radioactive, and if your reactor explodes, it will basically just float around the Earth and, at some point, get close enough to the atmosphere — it depends on the orbit — and then, over time, it will close up and be there. But the good news is, radioactivity decreases with the square root of the distance. If you are farther away, it doesn’t really matter. But once it hits the atmosphere, then we can have all kinds of fallout. That’s just physics. Any mass, any particle that’s circling the Earth, will be caught by our gravity and pulled closer and closer over time until it burns up. It can be years. It can be decades up there, so with all the other debris that we already see from exploding satellites, the more material we use that is critical and unhealthy for humans, the more risk we have.”
Conclusion
As chips move into increasingly unforgiving environments, reliability can no longer be treated as a final qualification step. AI-driven design exploration and advanced simulation can help engineers identify vulnerabilities earlier, but physical testing remains essential for understanding how real hardware responds when multiple stresses collide. For extreme-environment electronics, the challenge is no longer simply designing chips that perform. It is proving they will keep performing when conditions are at their worst.

articles.title: Kioxia CM9-R 15.36TB E3.S NVMe SSD Review
articles.text:
Today we are looking at the Kioxia CM9-R 15.36TB E3.S PCIe Gen5 SSD. Compared with the 7.68TB CD9P-R we tested earlier we expect similar read speeds, but the CM9-R should offer better write speeds. As a result, it seems like something fun to review, so let us get to it.
Kioxia CM9-R 15.36TB E3.S NVMe SSD Overview
The silver faceplate features a blue-and-white Kioxia CM9 label. This EDSFF E3.S drive measures 7.5mm thick and provides 15.36TB of capacity. It is strange to think of that as a midrange or even lower capacity drive, but now that we are in the era of 245/256TB-class SSDs, it is where we are.
The protruding edge connector requires a compatible E3.S bay. Kioxia specifies PCIe Gen5 operation in either single x4 or dual x2 modes. With its CMx series of drives, Kioxia usually targets enterprise deployments where dual-port operation is important for high-availability arrays.
The black underside displays a white regulatory sticker and model information but not much else.
The following specification table covers the 15.36 TB E3.S configuration. Kioxia rates endurance at 1 DWPD with a five-year warranty.
| Specification | Kioxia CM9-R 15.36TB E3.S | 
|---|---|
| Tested model / firmware | KCM9XRJE15T3 / 15ETE105 | 
| Interface | PCIe 5.0, NVMe 2.0; single x4 or dual x2 | 
| Flash | BiCS FLASH generation 8 TLC | 
| Endurance / warranty | 1 DWPD / 5 years | 
| Rated sequential read / write | Up to 14,800 / 11,000 MB/s | 
| Rated 4K random read / write | Up to 3,400,000 / 540,000 IOPS | 
| Dimensions | 112.75 x 76 x 7.5 mm | 
Normally, we have slides for the drive, but we did not have spec slides from the launch here, so we made a table. We covered the launch a few quarters ago, but now is our opportunity to test one out, so let us get to that.

articles.title: Exploitation of Citrix NetScaler Zero-Day Hits Appliances Patched Days Earlier
articles.text:
Citrix NetScaler administrators scrambled over the weekend to protect their appliances after exploitation of a new zero-day vulnerability began.
Administrators initially reported reboots of fully patched NetScaler systems on Friday, and Citrix soon confirmed the existence of another zero-day exploited in the wild.
According to Citrix, the new vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779 and classified as high severity, is a memory overflow issue affecting NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway instances configured as a SAML SP or SAML IdP.
“Citrix has observed targeted attacks on unmitigated NetScaler deployments which can lead to Denial of Service,” Citrix explained in a blog post. “If the condition is triggered repeatedly, the service may remain unavailable. Our analysis indicates that this issue affects service availability, and we have not identified an impact on the integrity of customer data.”
The attacks were spotted just days after NetScaler administrators were warned about two actively exploited zero-days, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, which forced some customers to pull the plug.
While Citrix describes CVE-2026-88779 as a DoS vulnerability, there is some indication it may also be exploitable for remote code execution.
Security researcher Kevin Beaumont, who dubbed the vulnerability PitScaler 2 (CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 are dubbed PitScaler), confirmed seeing exploitation attempts against patched honeypot instances. Beaumont also reported that one of his honeypots was running a downloaded malware binary.
Reddit users initially reported that NetScaler appliances already updated to the latest version in response to the CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 attacks kept rebooting. Logs reviewed by affected admins showed authentication requests carrying shell commands hidden in the username field and meant to fetch and run a malicious script.
One user who obtained the script said it tries to plant web shells, survive reboots, and upload the appliance’s configuration and backups, but cautioned that there was no proof the script actually ran.
Before patches arrived, admins complained about support queues that lasted hours and about interim workarounds that sometimes failed to stop the crashes.
CISA added CVE-2026-88779 to its KEV catalog on October 4, instructing federal agencies to address it by October 7. This is the sixth exploited NetScaler vulnerability CISA added to its catalog in 2026.
UPDATE: Security firm WatchTowr told SecurityWeek that it has successfully reproduced CVE-2026-88779 and determined that it’s a DoS bug that can only be used to crash systems. The company suspects it has been used to purposefully crash machines, making exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 faster.

articles.title: A Decade of Industrial Grade Linux: How the Civil Infrastructure Platform Is Securing Mission-Critical Systems
articles.text:
A Decade of Industrial Grade Linux: How the Civil Infrastructure Platform Is Securing Mission-Critical Systems
Hilary Carter | 06 October 2026
The global systems that power our communities, from energy grids and transportation networks to water distribution and healthcare systems, are built to last for decades. Yet as physical equipment becomes increasingly software-defined, managing those deployments over multi-decade lifecycles presents a profound operational challenge.
Today, I’m excited to share a new report from LF Research that provides an up-close view into how one project has been able to address this challenge head-on. In a new qualitative research report, Civil Infrastructure Platform: Industrial Grade Linux at 10, readers can take a deep dive into how open source collaboration transforms the software maintenance burden into a shared, manageable baseline for the entire industrial sector. Additionally, more projects than just the Civil Infrastructure Platform (CIP) have benefitted from this work, most notably the Linux kernel project. And as the report’s author, it was a great opportunity for me to get to know this community and to be inspired by their impact and year-over-year commitments, especially on the occasion of the project’s 10th anniversary.
Here are a few of the key findings from our latest collaboration with the CIP project, starting with the scope of industrial infrastructure spending and the need for software for decades-long time horizons, followed by the fundamental challenges around which CIP project leaders collaborate.
As global infrastructure investments reach unprecedented levels, software longevity has evolved into a core economic requirement. The report reveals that standard consumer-grade software support windows create a severe operational structural disconnect when paired with long-living physical assets. Traditionally, organizations spent massive corporate engineering resources tracking identical security bugs and maintaining custom, siloed Linux distributions in isolation.
To bridge this operational gap, CIP established a 10-year Super Long-Term Support (SLTS) kernel baseline. The report details how CIP converts standard Linux Long-Term Support kernels into robust, 10-year maintainable platforms, protecting asset-heavy industries from premature and disruptive software migration cycles.
Beyond technical longevity, the report reveals how open source collaboration mutualizes regulatory compliance, particularly as strict global mandates take effect. For example, under regulations like the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), non-compliance penalties can reach up to €15 million or 2.5% of global annual turnover. By pooling technical bandwidth and security expertise, CIP member organizations collectively navigate stringent compliance mandates, converting massive individual legal liabilities into shared, automated technical workflows.
Throughout the report, key figures from Cybertrust Japan, Renesas, Siemens, Texas Instruments, and Toshiba shared their reflections on what is working well today and what they would like to see in the future to make sure the CIP project is sustainable for the next ten years. The following recommendations surfaced from the research discussions. They summarize what company engineers and project leaders alike can do to derive maximum benefit in terms of cost savings, cybersecurity, shared expertise, and sustainability of civil infrastructure:
- Transition from consumers to active stewards: Shift engineering strategy from passive software consumption to active governance to help guide technical roadmaps and share long-term validation burdens.
- Implement security by design: Rely on verified industrial baselines that provide predictable stability updates over multi-decade horizons to streamline ongoing vulnerability management.
- Mutualize regulatory risk: Leverage pre-competitive, shared consortium frameworks to fulfill certification requirements and lower compliance overhead.
- Drive hardware alignment: Engage silicon suppliers directly with open software communities to bridge physical hardware lifecycles with stable, long-term software releases.
To the leaders of the CIP, who have dedicated engineering resources and their valuable time to this initiative, I would like to express my gratitude for their generosity and trust to foray into the benefits and pain points facing their organizations, as many of them did in support of our previous qualitative study in 2025 on CRA best practices. Without their active community stewardship and sponsorship of Linux Foundation’s collaborative support programs, and their commitment to engaging in the qualitative interview process, LF Research would not have had the opportunity to shine a light on the incredibly important work they do to support industrial grade Linux across modern infrastructure.
We invite asset operators, silicon manufacturers, and enterprise technologists to explore this research report, along with our comprehensive library of empirical studies, datasets, and insights, and to engage in projects of consequence like CIP. Discover the full report and our broader collection by visiting Linux Foundation Research.

articles.title: Xing-Gründer plant neuen 10-Euro-Tarif: „Es ist ein kompletter Angriff auf die Telekom und viele andere“
articles.text:
Simsalasim: Xing-Gründer plant unbegrenzten Datentarif für 10 Euro in 100 Ländern
Wer regelmäßig international reist, kennt das Problem: Außerhalb der EU sind Anrufe und Datenvolumen plötzlich nicht mehr im Mobilfunkvertrag enthalten. Das Verschicken von Urlaubsfotos, das Checken von E-Mails oder das Googeln des nächsten Restaurants kann so schnell ein kleines Vermögen kosten. Xing-Gründer Lars Hinrichs will eine dauerhafte Lösung bieten und mit seinem Mobilfunk-Startup Simsalasim unbegrenztes Datenvolumen in 100 Ländern ermöglichen – für nur zehn Euro pro Monat.
Mobiles Datenvolumen ist auf Reisen teuer
In Urlaubsländern wie Italien oder Portugal sind Smartphone-Nutzer:innen durch das EU-Daten-Roaming verwöhnt. Es gewährleistet, dass Reisende ihren mobilen Datentarif grundsätzlich zu denselben Bedingungen nutzen können wie zu Hause. Diese Regelung gilt in allen 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten sowie in Island, Liechtenstein und Norwegen. Seit Januar 2026 gehören auch Moldau und die Ukraine dazu. Abgedeckt sind zudem Überseegebiete wie die Kanarischen Inseln, die Azoren, Martinique und La Réunion. Großbritannien ist seit dem Brexit zwar kein EU-Mitglied mehr. Trotzdem bieten die großen deutschen Anbieter hier weiterhin Daten-Roaming ohne Zusatzkosten.
EU-Roaming ist seit 2017 möglich und wurde 2022 erneuert. Außerhalb Europas ist allerdings weiterhin ein Zusatztarif nötig. Wer im Winter zum Beispiel in Südafrika mobile Daten über die deutsche SIM-Karte nutzt, zahlt je nach Anbieter mehrere Euro pro Megabyte. Die Bundesnetzagentur empfiehlt deshalb, die Auslandspreise vorab zu prüfen. Auslandstarife von Mobilfunk- und E-SIM-Anbietern lassen sich zwar unkompliziert buchen, können aber ebenfalls schnell sehr teuer werden. Wer mehrere Länder nacheinander bereist, kann zum Beispiel bei der Telekom zusätzlich zum Vertrag den „Travel Mobil“-Tarif wählen. Er deckt die Ländergruppen 2 und 3 ab und kostet rund 100 Euro pro Monat.
Simsalasim will Telekom und Co. angreifen
Xing-Gründer Hinrichs will Reisenden mit Simsalasim bald eine praktischere und günstigere Option bieten – einen Tarif für zehn Euro im Monat, der nahezu weltweit nutzbar ist. Hinrichs saß über ein Jahrzehnt im Telekom-Aufsichtsrat und schied Anfang 2025 aus. Jetzt will er die Branche umkrempeln. Der Grund: „Im Bereich Telekom gab es keine wirkliche Innovation in den letzten zwanzig, dreißig Jahren. Es ging immer nur um Zeit oder Daten im Verhältnis zum Preis“, sagte er gegenüber der FAZ. Simsalasim sei deshalb „ein kompletter Angriff auf die Telekom, Vodafone und viele, viele andere.“
Der Tarif soll unbegrenzt mobile Daten ohne Drosselung bieten und in etwa 50 Ländern zusätzlich unbegrenzte Telefonate und SMS ermöglichen. Kund:innen aktivieren ihn über eine E-SIM. Die Nutzung des Smartphones als Hotspot sei allerdings ausgeschlossen, sodass Personen, die remote arbeiten, weiterhin einen zusätzlichen Tarif buchen müssten. Aber wie will Hinrichs dieses deutlich günstigere Angebot umsetzen? „Wir haben keine Funkmasten und betreiben keine klassischen Handy-Shops“, sagte er der Bild-Zeitung. Simsalasim kaufe in Deutschland stattdessen Netzkapazitäten von Telefónica ein.
Xing-Gründer plant ein „One-Person-Unicorn“
Statt auf ein eigenes Funknetz setzt Hinrichs auf Software und KI. Laut Bild arbeite das Unternehmen mit nur 25 Beschäftigten. Softwareentwicklung, Abrechnung, Marketing und Kundenservice sollen weitgehend automatisiert werden. Sein Ziel sei es, die Funktionen eines Telekommunikationsunternehmens mithilfe von KI abzubilden. Er verfolge damit auch das Konzept des „One-Person-Unicorns“, also eines Startups mit einer Bewertung von mehr als einer Milliarde Dollar, extrem wenig Personal – und im Idealfall nur einem Gründer. Ob ihm das mit Simsalasim gelingt, bleibt abzuwarten.

articles.title: Le cinéma français en danger ? Canal+ tire la sonnette d'alarme
articles.text:
Ce lundi 5 octobre, face à Marc-Olivier Fogiel sur RTL, le patron du groupe Canal+, Maxime Saada, n’a pas mâché ses mots au moment d’évoquer le projet de loi de finances 2027 porté par le gouvernement de Sébastien Lecornu. L’exécutif prévoit en effet d’aligner la TVA des chaînes payantes en temps réel sur celle des plateformes de streaming à la demande, la faisant grimper de 10 % à 20 %.
Canal+ chiffre le surcoût à 200 millions d’euros par an, une somme que le groupe dit ne pas pouvoir absorber : selon Maxime Saada, l’activité en France est « péniblement rentable ». Si la hausse est votée, Maxime Saada prévient que Canal+ la répercutera, jusque sur le financement du cinéma français.
Canal+ menace d’augmenter ses prix et de réduire ses coûts
Selon Maxime Saada, la mesure doit rapporter environ 300 millions d’euros à l’État, mais elle en fera perdre en réalité, avec des suppressions de postes dans l’Hexagone et-outre mer. Il la juge « anti économique ». Si le Parlement valide la mesure, Canal+ annonce plusieurs contre-mesures :
- Abonnements en hausse : les tarifs pour les abonnés grimperont d’environ 10 %, soit un peu moins de 3 euros par mois sur une formule à 29 euros. Maxime Saada précise que la hausse n’interviendra « pas avant 2028 ou 2029 » : près de 90 % des abonnés sont engagés pour un ou deux ans, et leur tarif ne peut pas changer en cours de contrat.
- Licenciements en vue : un plan social au sein de la branche française n’est pas exclu pour compenser le choc fiscal.
- Avenir en France : Maxime Saada estime que « la question de la pérennité de Canal+ en France se pose ». Dans un communiqué publié la semaine dernière, le groupe, présent dans près de 70 pays, annonçait déjà qu’il « accélérera sa stratégie de déploiement à l’international ».
Le financement du cinéma français en jeu
Maxime Saada met surtout en avant le financement du cinéma français. Historiquement, Canal+ est le premier financeur privé du cinéma français. Fin juillet, le groupe s’est engagé à investir 980 millions d’euros entre 2028 et 2032 dans le cinéma français et européen, soit environ 196 millions d’euros par an, en échange de la TVA réduite et de fenêtres de diffusion privilégiées.
Maxime Saada rappelle aussi que Canal+ est « le premier financier du sport français », avec notamment le Top 14 et la Ligue des champions. Dans le même communiqué, Canal+ juge la proposition du gouvernement « incohérente et inconséquente », moins d’un an après la confirmation de son taux de TVA à 10 % par l’administration fiscale. Pour le groupe, l’État s’apprête à faire exactement l’inverse.
Maxime Saada qualifie la mesure de « décision absurde, qui n’a aucun sens économique » et qui « ne peut être que politique ». Il laisse entendre que le groupe est visé à travers son premier actionnaire, le groupe Bolloré, contrôlé par la famille de Vincent Bolloré.
Bercy justifie la mesure par une simplification. Le ministère de l’Économie juge la distinction entre télévision en direct et contenus à la demande « de plus en plus artificielle » et estime que ce taux réduit est « très peu répandu en Europe ».
Faute d’avoir été entendu par Bercy, Maxime Saada compte désormais « discuter avec les parlementaires » qui vont examiner le projet de loi de finances. « Rien n’est joué, nous espérons bien faire changer la trajectoire de ce texte », a-t-il assuré.
